docs.title: Open Data Stack (odctl)
docs.text:
Run an open data stack on your machine, with its services already connected, from one command.

odctl is a command-line tool that runs an open data stack on your machine with Docker Compose. You name the profiles you want, such as kafka-lite or airflow, and odctl starts them together with the services they depend on.

A Compose file of your own is enough for one small project. Why odctl explains what odctl adds when several projects need different parts of the stack.

docs.text:
Each command has its own section in the CLI reference, with its options and examples. The Example column links to a page that runs the command and shows its output, and Getting Started runs them in order on one profile.

docs.text:
Usage: odctl [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

 odctl: run an open data stack on your machine, with its services already
 connected, from one command.

 Commands list the profiles, start and stop them with Docker Compose, and show
 what is running.

╭─ Options ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --install-completion          Install completion for the current shell.      │
│ --show-completion             Show completion for the current shell, to copy │

╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Global Options ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --verbose                    Enable debug-level logging across all commands. │
│ --workspace  -w      <path>  Path to the odctl workspace directory (default: │
│                              ./.odctl).                                      │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Inspection & Info ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ list      List all available profiles and their capabilities.                │
│ explain   Explain the details, services, images, and dependencies of a       │
│           profile.                                                           │
│ ps        List Docker containers managed by the Open Data Stack.             │
│ info      Show the installed odctl version and whether Docker is reachable.  │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Workspace ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ init      Initialize a local .odctl workspace for custom configurations.     │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Cluster Lifecycle ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ pull      Pre-fetch Docker images without starting the containers.           │
│ up        Launch Open Data profiles.                                         │

╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

   # View all profiles and exposed ports

   $ odctl list -d


   # See exactly what the kafka-lite profile provisions

   $ odctl explain kafka-lite

   $ odctl up flink-lite kafka-lite spark-lite


   # Complete teardown and wipe all data

   $ odctl down --all --volumes

docs.title: odctl init
docs.text:
Usage: odctl init [OPTIONS]

 Initialize a local .odctl workspace for custom configurations.

 Copies the bundled docker-compose files, configs, and `.env` template into a
 local `./.odctl/` directory. You can then edit these files directly to
 customize the stack.

╭─ Options ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --force  -f        Wipe out the existing workspace and recreate it from      │
│                    scratch.                                                  │
│ --yes    -y        Answer yes to the confirmation prompt, for scripts and    │
│                    CI.                                                       │
│ --help             Show this message and exit.                               │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

 Examples:

   # Initialize a new workspace in ./.odctl/

   $ odctl init


   # Recreate workspace, overwriting any local changes

   $ odctl init --force


   # The same, without the prompt, as in a script

   $ odctl init --force --yes

docs.title: odctl pull
docs.text:
Usage: odctl pull [OPTIONS] [profiles]...

 Pre-fetch Docker images without starting the containers.

 Useful for downloading heavy images (like Spark, Flink, Kafka) ahead of time,
 or for fetching a tag that changed in the registry before launching.

╭─ Arguments ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│   profiles      <str>  Specific profiles to pull images for.                 │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

│ --all   -a        Pull images for ALL available profiles in the registry.    │
│ --help            Show this message and exit.                                │

   $ odctl pull --all


   # Pre-fetch images just for Flink and Kafka

docs.title: odctl up
docs.text:
Usage: odctl up [OPTIONS] {profiles}...

 Launch Open Data profiles.

 Resolves dependencies for the requested profiles and brings up the required
 Docker Compose stacks in the correct topological order.

 Refuses to start if the images for the resolved TAG are not published,
 naming the tag rather than leaving Docker to report a missing manifest.
 Warns about any service whose declared profile belongs to another compose
 file, since the planner will never start it.

╭─ Arguments ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ *    profiles      <str>  One or more profiles to launch (for example,       │
│                           'ch-lite', 'kafka-lite').                          │
│                           [required]                                         │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Options ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --dry-run          Preview the execution plan without actually starting      │
│                    anything.                                                 │
│ --pull             Pull the images again before starting, to fetch a tag     │
│                    that changed in the registry.                             │
│ --help             Show this message and exit.                               │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

 Examples:

   # Launch Clickhouse, Flink, and their dependencies

   $ odctl up ch-lite flink-lite


   # Preview what would be launched for Airflow

   $ odctl up airflow --dry-run


   # Pull the images again before launching

   $ odctl up kafka-lite --pull

docs.title: odctl down
docs.text:
Usage: odctl down [OPTIONS] [profiles]...

 Stop and remove profile containers and networks.

 Tears down the requested profiles. Data kept inside a container is removed
 with it.
 Unnamed volumes stay on disk, unused.
 Use --volumes to also remove the volumes, such as the shared jar volume.

╭─ Arguments ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│   profiles      <str>  Specific profiles to stop.                            │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Options ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --all      -a        Stop ALL running profiles.                              │
│ --volumes  -v        Also remove named volumes, including the shared jar     │
│                      volume once no other profile uses it.                   │
│ --dry-run            Preview the teardown plan without actually stopping     │
│                      anything.                                               │
│ --yes      -y        Answer yes to the confirmation prompt, for scripts and  │
│                      CI.                                                     │
│ --help               Show this message and exit.                             │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

 Examples:

   # Stop specific profile(s)

   $ odctl down kafka-lite


   # Stop all running profiles

   $ odctl down --all


   # Complete teardown and wipe all data

   $ odctl down --all -v


   # The same, without the prompt, as in a script

   $ odctl down --all -v --yes

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page installs odctl, starts a first profile, runs each command on it and stops it. It needs no earlier page. The recording shows the main steps: install odctl, preview a profile, start it, list the containers and stop them.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Docker Engine or Docker Desktop, running. Give Docker 8 to 16 GB of memory.
  • Python 3.10 or later.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
odctl is a command-line tool, so install it into its own environment with uv or pipx:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:install
uv tool install odctl
# or
pipx install odctl

pip install odctl also works. odctl --help then lists the commands.

docs.title: Create a Workspace
docs.text:
Run this in the folder of your project:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:init
odctl init

It prints Workspace initialized! with the path of the new folder. The command copies the compose files and their settings into .odctl in the current directory, and writes .odctl/.env with TAG set to the CLI version. odctl reads from .odctl whenever it exists, so you can edit any file there. Workspace explains what changes with and without it, and how to customise it.

docs.title: Start a Profile
docs.text:
A profile is a named group of services that start together. This lists every profile, with its parent stack and a description:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:list
odctl list

Add -d to list each profile's services and host ports as well:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:list-details
odctl list -d

This shows what one profile runs:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:explain
odctl explain kafka-lite

It prints a panel for kafka-lite: the parent stack kafka, the compose file, the profile it requires (deps), the containers connect, kafka, kafka-ui and karapace with their images, the host ports and how to reach each service. This shows the profiles kafka-lite would start, in order, without starting anything:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:dry-run
odctl up kafka-lite --dry-run

The dry run prints which compose files and profiles it would start:

Start it:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:up
odctl up kafka-lite

odctl starts the profiles kafka-lite depends on first, then Kafka. It waits until the services are running, and healthy where they define a health check, then prints All requested profiles successfully started!. The Messaging page lists the same addresses as odctl explain.

docs.title: See What Is Running
docs.text:
This prints the installed CLI version and whether Docker is reachable:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:info
odctl info

The output has two lines: CLI Version: with the version, and Docker Daemon: ✅ Reachable. This lists the containers of a profile, with their state, health and ports:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:ps
odctl ps kafka-lite

It prints a table with one row per container:

┏━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Container ┃ Service  ┃ State   ┃ Health  ┃ Ports           ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ connect   │ connect  │ running │ -       │ 8083 → 8083/tcp │
│ kafka     │ kafka    │ running │ -       │ 9092 → 9092/tcp │
│ kafka-ui  │ kafka-ui │ running │ -       │ 8086 → 8080/tcp │
│ karapace  │ karapace │ running │ healthy │ 8081 → 8081/tcp │
└───────────┴──────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────────────┘

A dash under Health means the service has no health check. This lists every container odctl manages, from every profile, including one-shot containers that have finished, such as odctl-init-deps:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:ps-all
odctl ps --all

This prints the last three log lines of one service, connect:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:logs
odctl logs kafka-lite -s connect -n 3

Each line starts with the service name, such as connect | [2026-10-24 05:14:03,065] INFO [Worker clientId=connect-connect:8083, .... Leave out -s connect to read every service of the profile, and add -f to follow the logs until you press Ctrl+C. This prints the last two lines written between ten minutes and one second ago, each with a timestamp before it:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:logs-time
odctl logs kafka-lite -s connect --since 10m --until 1s -t -n 2

--since and --until each take a time such as 2026-10-24T05:00:00 or a duration before now such as 10m.

docs.title: Restart a Profile
docs.text:
This restarts the profile's containers and keeps them, with their data:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:restart
odctl restart kafka-lite

It prints Restarting containers... and Restart complete. A restart does not apply an edit to a compose file or .env. odctl recreate replaces the containers to apply one, as Apply a Change explains with examples. odctl pull downloads a profile's images before you start it, as Which Images Run shows.

docs.title: Stop a Profile
docs.text:
This prints what odctl down would stop, without stopping anything:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:down-dry-run
odctl down kafka-lite --dry-run

This stops the profile and removes its containers:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:down
odctl down kafka-lite

It prints Teardown complete. The data inside the containers goes with them, as Where Data Lives explains. It leaves the profiles that kafka-lite depends on in place, as Which Containers a Command Touches explains. This stops every profile and also removes the named volumes, such as the shared jar volume odctl-shared-deps. It asks Are you sure? first, and stops only after you answer y:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:down-all
odctl down --all --volumes

In a script, --yes answers the prompt:

docs/snippets/getting-started/commands.sh:down-all-yes
odctl down --all --volumes --yes

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: This page explains how odctl chooses, starts and reaches its services, where their data lives and how to change them. It builds on Getting Started.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text: A profile is a named group of services that start together, such as kafka-lite or airflow. odctl uses Docker Compose profiles: each service in a compose file lists the profiles it belongs to. registry.yml lists every profile, the compose file it lives in and the profiles it depends on. A tool with a small and a clustered form has two profiles, -lite and -full, such as kafka-lite with one broker and kafka-full with three. odctl list prints every profile, and Profiles has a page for each one.

docs.title: What odctl up Does
docs.text:
Take odctl up flink-lite as an example. Flink keeps its tables in Iceberg, so it needs the Iceberg REST catalog. The catalog keeps its metadata in PostgreSQL and its files in SeaweedFS, an object store with an S3 API. All of them need the shared jars in deps.

odctl reads these links from registry.yml and starts the profiles from left to right:

  1. deps copies connectors and jars into a shared Docker volume, creates the odctl network, and exits.
  2. postgres and storage start, and odctl waits until they are healthy.
  3. catalog starts once both are healthy.
  4. flink-lite starts last.

This command prints the plan without starting anything:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:dry-run
odctl up flink-lite --dry-run

It lists each compose file with its profiles, from compose-deps.yml with deps to compose-flink.yml with flink-lite. Each profile page lists what its profile also starts.

docs.title: Dependencies and the Start Order
docs.text:
Each profile lists the profiles it needs under depends_on in registry.yml. odctl follows those lists from the profiles you name, one level at a time, until no new profile appears. It then sorts the result: deps first, postgres and storage next, catalog after them, and every other profile last, in alphabetical order.

The profiles are then grouped by compose file, in that order, and each file is started with one docker compose up --wait. That call returns once every service it started is running, and healthy where it has a health check, so a file starts only after the files before it are ready. deps is the exception: it starts attached, because its init container copies the jars and exits, and --wait treats an exiting container as a failure.

docs.title: Before Anything Starts
docs.text:
odctl up checks four things before it starts a container. The diagram shows them in order, and the list below explains each one:

  1. Docker is reachable. If not, it stops.
  2. Every profile you name is in registry.yml. An unknown name stops it, with the name in the error.
  3. Every service can be started. A service that declares a profile owned by another compose file would never start, so odctl warns about it and carries on.
  4. odctl's own images exist for the tag. It resolves TAG as compose does and asks the registry for each odctl image that is not already on your machine. If the registry says one is missing, odctl stops and names the tag, rather than leaving Docker to fail on one service. If the registry cannot be reached, it starts anyway, so a machine with no network can run images it pulled before.

docs.title: Which Containers a Command Touches
docs.text:
down, ps, logs, restart and recreate act only on the profiles you name, not on their dependencies. odctl down flink-lite stops Flink and leaves PostgreSQL, SeaweedFS and the catalog running for other profiles. odctl finds the containers by their compose labels: the project name starts with odctl-, and the service belongs to one of the named profiles.

There is one exception. When a profile depends on another profile in the same compose file, both are included, because compose refuses a command on a service whose dependency is left out. odctl down --volumes removes the shared deps volume and the odctl network only when no other profile has a container left.

docs.title: How You Reach a Service
docs.text:
Every service publishes its ports on the host at 127.0.0.1 only, so a browser or client on your machine uses http://127.0.0.1:<port>, and other machines on your network cannot reach them. This works the same on macOS, Linux and WSL2: Docker Desktop forwards the port to the host's 127.0.0.1, and WSL2 forwards it to Windows' localhost. To open a port to your network, remove 127.0.0.1: from its line in .odctl/compose-*.yml and run odctl recreate <profile>. Each profile page lists the ports.

Inside Docker, services reach each other by name on the odctl network, for example http://catalog:8181 or broker-1:19092 for Kafka. A container of your own reaches them the same way when it joins that network:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:reach
docker run --rm --network odctl curlimages/curl:8.17.0 -s http://catalog:8181/v1/config

With the catalog profile running, it prints the catalog's configuration as JSON, which starts with {"defaults":.

docs.title: Where Data Lives
docs.text:
Most services keep their data inside their containers. PostgreSQL, SeaweedFS, ClickHouse and Fluss's ZooKeeper are the exception: their images declare a data volume, so Docker gives each of these containers an unnamed volume, which a recreate passes on to the new container.

Command Containers Your data odctl restart kept kept odctl recreate replaced lost, except in PostgreSQL, SeaweedFS, ClickHouse and ZooKeeper, which keep their volumes odctl down removed lost; the unnamed volumes stay on disk, unused odctl down --volumes removed, with the unnamed volumes and the odctl-shared-deps volume lost

A database, a bucket, a topic or an Iceberg table therefore lasts until its profile is stopped, and every odctl up is a clean start. odctl down --volumes also frees the disk the unnamed volumes hold. The odctl-shared-deps volume holds only jars, so keeping it makes the next start faster.

docs.title: Which Images Run
docs.text:
Most services run their project's official image, pinned to an exact version. odctl builds five images of its own and publishes them to ghcr.io/jaehyeon-kim/odctl/:

Image Contents deps Connectors, jars and the Prometheus JMX agent, including the Iceberg REST catalog and the Kafka Connect Iceberg sink postgres PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector, pg_textsearch and PostGIS airflow Airflow with the MLflow and Feast clients and the model runtimes mlflow The MLflow server and model server with the model runtimes spark Spark with the Python clients jobs use

These five are tagged with the CLI version through TAG. Workspace explains how TAG is set with and without odctl init.

odctl up downloads the images it does not have. To download them first, for example before you go offline, pull a profile and the profiles it depends on:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:pull
odctl pull catalog

It prints Fetching images for each compose file, a Pulled line for each image and All images pulled successfully!. odctl pull --all pulls the images of every profile, which is many GB. To fetch newer images of the same tags as you start a profile, add --pull:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:up-pull
odctl up catalog --pull

docs.title: Workspace
docs.text: odctl runs from one of two places: the files bundled with the CLI, or a workspace that odctl init copies them into.

docs.title: With and Without odctl init
docs.text:
Without a workspace With a workspace Files odctl reads the compose files and registry.yml inside the installed package the copies in .odctl in the current directory Image tag of odctl's own images the CLI version the CLI version, written to .odctl/.env as TAG Your changes none; the package is replaced on every upgrade any file in .odctl After a CLI upgrade new files and images at once the old files and images, with a warning on every command until odctl init --force

A TAG set in the shell overrides both. This shows the image the postgres profile would run with another tag, without changing the workspace:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:tag-override
TAG=1.1.0 odctl explain postgres | grep odctl/postgres

It prints the panel's line for the postgres container, with the image ghcr.io/jaehyeon-kim/odctl/postgres:1.1.0.

odctl looks for .odctl in the current directory. --workspace PATH uses the workspace folder at PATH instead, such as ../shared/.odctl, so one workspace can serve several projects. It goes before the command:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:workspace-flag
odctl --workspace ./.odctl ps catalog

docs.title: Customise It
docs.text:
odctl init copies everything odctl runs into .odctl. It copies only files that are missing, so running it again keeps your edits.

File What to change compose-*.yml Host ports, memory limits and environment variables of each service registry.yml The profiles, their compose files and their dependencies .env TAG, the time zone of the services that read it (TZ, UTC by default), extra Python packages for Airflow (_AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS) and the MLflow services (_MLOPS_PIP_DEPS), and the model the MLflow model server serves (MODEL_URI) grafana/dashboards/ The Grafana dashboard for each service trino/rules.json Trino's file-based access control evidently/config.yaml The Evidently server's settings

docs.title: Apply a Change
docs.text:
A restart keeps the container, so it does not apply an edited compose file or .env. Run odctl recreate <profile> to replace the profile's containers from their current definition. Add --pull to fetch the images again first:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:recreate-pull
odctl recreate catalog --pull

Recreating discards the data inside those containers, with the exceptions that Where Data Lives lists. odctl restart <profile> is enough for files a service reads when it starts, such as trino/rules.json and the Grafana dashboards.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Each example edits the workspace, then applies the change. sed -i.bak works with both GNU and macOS sed, and keeps the original as a .bak file.

Give SeaweedFS 2 GB instead of 512 MB, for example when several projects share it. SeaweedFS is a Go program, and GOMEMLIMIT is a soft memory limit: as the memory the Go runtime manages nears it, the garbage collector runs more often and returns memory to the system sooner. It is three quarters of mem_limit, so change both:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:seaweed-memory
sed -i.bak -e '/^  seaweed:/,/^  [a-z]/ s/mem_limit: 512m/mem_limit: 2g/' \
  -e '/^  seaweed:/,/^  [a-z]/ s/GOMEMLIMIT: 384MiB/GOMEMLIMIT: 1536MiB/' .odctl/compose-infra.yml
odctl recreate storage
docker inspect seaweed --format '{{.HostConfig.Memory}}'

The last command prints 2147483648, which is 2 GB in bytes.

Publish Trino on port 8180 instead of 8080, when another program already uses 8080:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:trino-port
sed -i.bak 's/"127.0.0.1:8080:8080" # Trino/"127.0.0.1:8180:8080" # Trino/' .odctl/compose-analytics.yml
odctl recreate trino
docker port trino

The last command prints 8080/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:8180.

Install extra Python packages in the Airflow container, for DAGs that import them:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:airflow-deps
sed -i.bak 's/^_AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS=.*/_AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS="dateparser==1.4.3"/' .odctl/.env
odctl recreate airflow
docker exec airflow python -c "import dateparser; print(dateparser.__version__)"

The last command prints 1.4.3.

Install an extra Python package in the MLflow containers, for a model that imports it:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:mlops-deps
sed -i.bak 's/^_MLOPS_PIP_DEPS=.*/_MLOPS_PIP_DEPS="tabulate==0.9.0"/' .odctl/.env
odctl recreate mlflow
docker exec mlflow-serve python -c "import tabulate; print(tabulate.__version__)"

The last command prints 0.9.0. _AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS and _MLOPS_PIP_DEPS both install their packages from PyPI again in every new container: at the first odctl up, after odctl recreate, and after odctl down and odctl up. _AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS is for the Airflow containers. _MLOPS_PIP_DEPS is for the mlflow and mlflow-serve containers, for example a library a served model needs to load. odctl restart keeps the container, so the packages stay. Each new container needs PyPI, and pinned versions (transformers==5.20.2) keep the installed packages the same.

Set the time zone of the services that read TZ, here the MLflow containers:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:timezone
sed -i.bak 's/^TZ=.*/TZ=Australia\/Sydney/' .odctl/.env
odctl recreate mlflow
docker exec mlflow date +%Z

The last command prints AEDT from October to April and AEST for the rest of the year. PostgreSQL reads TZ only when it creates its data folder, and a recreate keeps that folder, so its time zone changes after odctl down postgres and odctl up postgres. MODEL_URI in .env sets the model mlflow-serve serves, as MLflow Tracking and Model Serving shows.

Create a bucket before its profile exists, for example for a project that has no profile. seaweed-init creates a fixed list of buckets, and .odctl/seaweed/s3.json gives the login user the Admin action, which creating a bucket needs. This runs boto3 in a container on the odctl network, where seaweed:8333 resolves, and prints the buckets, which now include desflow:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:create-bucket
docker run --rm -i --network odctl python:3.12-slim \
  sh -c 'pip install -q --root-user-action=ignore boto3==1.43.118 && python -' <<'PY'
import boto3
s3 = boto3.client("s3", endpoint_url="http://seaweed:8333", region_name="us-east-1",
                  aws_access_key_id="user", aws_secret_access_key="password")
s3.create_bucket(Bucket="desflow")
print(sorted(b["Name"] for b in s3.list_buckets()["Buckets"]))
PY

Two other ways exist. weed shell inside the seaweed container runs s3.bucket.create -name desflow, the command seaweed-init runs. Adding the name to BUCKETS in .odctl/compose-infra.yml creates it at every start of the storage profile. An upgrade needs odctl init --force, which removes that edit.

docs.title: Trino Access Rules
docs.text: The shipped trino/rules.json grants every identity full table privileges and denies analyst schema ownership. Add your own table rules there for row filtering and column masking, then restart Trino.

docs.title: Start Again
docs.text:
odctl init --force deletes .odctl and copies the bundled files again, with TAG set to the current CLI version. Your edits are lost, so it asks for confirmation first. In a script, --yes answers the prompt:

docs/snippets/how-it-works/commands.sh:init-force
odctl init --force --yes

docs.title: Containers Exit or Docker Runs Out of Memory
docs.text: Each service has a memory limit, listed on its profile page. The limits of everything you start add up, and Docker needs that much memory available. Give Docker the memory that Getting Started names, start fewer profiles at once, or choose a lite profile over a full one. To lower a limit, edit mem_limit in the compose file in .odctl and run odctl recreate <profile>, as How It Works shows for SeaweedFS.

docs.title: Uploads Fail with HTTP 500 and Seaweed Exited with Code 137
docs.text: seaweed reached its memory limit while it buffered a large upload, and the kernel killed it. The client sees HTTP 500 and every profile that uses S3 loses its storage until the container starts again. docker inspect seaweed --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' prints true after such a kill. A model or file of several hundred MB can reach the limit. Raise mem_limit and GOMEMLIMIT together, as How It Works shows for 2 GB. A workspace made by a release before GOMEMLIMIT was added lacks it until you run odctl init --force, which Start Again describes.

docs.title: A Port Is Already in Use
docs.text: Every service publishes fixed host ports, listed on its profile page. If another program holds one, odctl up fails to start that service. Stop the other program, or change the host side of the port mapping in .odctl/compose-*.yml and run odctl recreate <profile>, as How It Works shows for Trino. Containers still reach each other on their internal ports, so only clients on your host need the new port.

docs.title: Use 127.0.0.1, Not localhost
docs.text: Host addresses in odctl explain and on these pages use 127.0.0.1. With IPv6 enabled in Docker, localhost can resolve to a service's IPv6 address, and services that listen on IPv4 only reset the connection. localhost works when Docker's IPv6 is off.

docs.title: No Published Image for a TAG
docs.text:
odctl up checks the images odctl builds before it starts anything. If the registry says an image for the resolved TAG does not exist, it stops with No published image for TAG=... and lists the missing images. An image already on your machine passes without a registry call. If the registry cannot be reached, odctl starts anyway and Docker reports what it finds.

The usual causes are a CLI version whose images are not published yet, or a TAG in .odctl/.env that you changed by hand. Set TAG to a published version in .odctl/.env, or install a CLI version whose images exist.

docs.title: Workspace TAG Differs from the CLI Version
docs.text: After you upgrade the CLI, every command except odctl init warns that .odctl/.env sets an older TAG. The workspace keeps the old profiles, images and compose files until you run odctl init --force. Start Again says what that command removes.

docs.title: A Service Is Up but Does Not Work
docs.text: odctl logs <profile> shows the logs of a profile's containers. Add -s <service> for one service, or -f to follow them. odctl ps --all shows every container odctl manages and its state.

docs.title: Older Messages Are Missing
docs.text: The Kafka brokers delete old messages, so a consumer that starts from the beginning of a topic sees only what is left. Keep Messages Longer gives the limits, shows how to read them and shows how to set retention.ms and retention.bytes to -1 on a topic that must keep everything.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Each release, newest first: what changed, then under Upgrading what to change in commands, workspaces or clients that use the previous release. Releases up to 1.0.2 are described on GitHub Releases.

docs.title: Version 1.2.1
docs.text:
recreate, restart and logs work on profiles from several compose files, init and down can skip their prompt, and the docs show every command with a runnable example.

  • odctl recreate, odctl restart and odctl logs work on profiles from more than one compose file, such as odctl recreate storage kafka-lite. They ran every file as one project, so recreate failed with Conflict. The container name "/seaweed" is already in use, and restart and logs left out the containers of all but one file. Each file now runs as its own project, as with odctl up. Apply a Change uses odctl recreate.
  • odctl init --force --yes and odctl down --all --volumes --yes run without asking Are you sure?, for scripts and CI. -y is the short form. See Stop a Profile and Start Again.
  • Getting Started runs every command on kafka-lite, with its output, and the home page lists each command with a link to its example.
  • Every guide ends with a Runnable Example that names the files to run. Rolling Windows is a page of its own, and the Flink push to Feast moved to Push Features from Flink SQL.
  • The animation on How It Works shows its four steps again. Since 1.1.0 it showed steps 1 to 3 for a moment each and then stayed on step 4, because one step was exported 2 pixels narrower and ffmpeg stopped at the change in size.
  • The Labs page is hidden until its first lab is published.

docs.title: Version 1.2.0
docs.text:
Flink can send rows to an HTTP API, Spark reads Kafka with no extra options, SeaweedFS survives uploads of large models, and the guides cover cases that real projects met.

  • Flink's SQL client has the HTTP connector. Push Features from Flink SQL pushes a feature value to Feast.
  • Spark has the Kafka connector and the Avro module, so a job reads a topic, including Avro records written with the schema registry, with no --packages option. See Read a Kafka Topic and Read Avro Records Written with the Schema Registry.
  • Keep Messages Longer shows the broker's one-day and 500 MB retention and how to turn both off for a topic. Troubleshooting lists the symptom.
  • seaweed sets GOMEMLIMIT to three quarters of its memory limit, so uploads of a model of a few hundred MB no longer end with HTTP 500 and a killed container. Troubleshooting says what to do when the limit is still reached, and How It Works changes both values together.
  • The MLflow guide has three new sections: Move the Alias to a New Version, which needs odctl restart mlflow, Load a Model from Your Machine and Serve a Model That Reads Online Features.
  • The docs now say that the packages in _MLOPS_PIP_DEPS are installed from PyPI again in every new mlflow and mlflow-serve container. How It Works lists when a new container is made.
  • How It Works shows how to create a bucket before its profile exists.
  • Rolling Windows shows that Flink SQL refuses two different OVER windows in one streaming query, and the two ways around it.
  • The Evidently guide says what Evidently does not estimate and why NannyML needs Python 3.12.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: • A workspace made by odctl init with an earlier release keeps its old compose-infra.yml, which has no GOMEMLIMIT for seaweed. Run odctl init --force to copy the new files; it replaces your edits, so keep a copy of them. Then run odctl recreate storage.

docs.title: Version 1.1.0
docs.text:
Every service is now reachable from your machine only, and the docs have a Roadmap and a Changelog.

  • Every published port binds to 127.0.0.1, on macOS, Linux and WSL2, so other machines on your network cannot reach the services. How You Reach a Service says how to open a port when you need to.
  • Kafka no longer publishes ports 29092, 29093 and 29094, which were listeners for a minikube cluster.
  • An odctl skill and llms.txt help an AI assistant choose a profile and reach its services. See Use It with an AI Assistant.
  • Eight guides show in a diagram how data moves between their services, and How It Works shows what odctl up checks and the order it starts services in. The end-to-end tests run every command the guides show.
  • The tables of odctl ps and odctl explain draw straight right borders on rows with port mappings.
  • odctl down --help says what --volumes removes.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
• To reach a service from another machine, run odctl init, remove 127.0.0.1: from the service's port line in .odctl/compose-*.yml, and run odctl recreate <profile>.
  • A Kafka client in minikube cannot use host.minikube.internal:29092 any more. Add a listener for it to the Kafka service in .odctl/compose-kafka.yml.
  • A workspace made by odctl init with an earlier release keeps its old compose files, which publish on all interfaces and include port 29092. Run odctl init --force to copy the new files; it replaces your edits.

docs.title: Why odctl
docs.text:
I like building demo apps, and each one needs a local environment to try things in. Docker and Docker Compose are good for that. Across several projects, though, it is not easy, and the setup drifts from one project to the next.

odctl is a CLI that manages Docker Compose services. It runs Compose files and selects services with Compose profiles. For one small project with two or three services, plain Compose is fine.

It starts to hurt when you have several projects. One needs Kafka, Flink and Iceberg. Another needs Spark and Trino but not Kafka. Each project ends up with its own Compose file, and over time they drift apart, for example when you upgrade image tags in one and forget the others. With odctl, the files live in one place. Each release fixes the image versions, and an end-to-end test runs every profile before it is published. A project just pins an odctl version.

The second part is the wiring, and odctl does it for you. When PostgreSQL first starts, it creates a database for each service that needs one, such as the Iceberg catalog, Airflow and MLflow. The Iceberg REST catalog keeps its tables in S3 storage (SeaweedFS), and Spark and Trino are already configured to use it. Kafka Connect, Flink and Spark also need connector jars with matching versions. odctl builds them once into a shared image, and each service takes the jars it needs from there. odctl up spark-lite starts PostgreSQL, the storage, the catalog and the shared jars first, and Prometheus already scrapes Kafka, Flink, Spark and ClickHouse.

The third part is day-to-day use. With several Compose files, it is hard to remember what is running and where. odctl has commands for that:

  • odctl list shows every profile and what it runs.
  • odctl explain spark-lite shows a profile's services, images, ports and the profiles it depends on.
  • odctl up spark-lite --dry-run shows what would start, in order, before anything starts.
  • odctl ps --all lists the running containers and their ports.
  • odctl logs spark-lite shows the logs of one profile.
  • odctl down --all stops everything.

Getting all of this right by hand takes time, and it is easy to break across projects.

I use odctl in my own projects: desflow starts the services of its tests and examples with it, and so do the demos in benchtop. It is useful for three kinds of project:

  • Data engineering. Streaming and batch pipelines on Kafka, Kafka Connect, Flink, Fluss and Spark, an Iceberg lakehouse queried with Trino, ClickHouse for analytics, Airflow and Temporal to run them, and lineage in Marquez and OpenMetadata.
  • ML and MLOps. MLflow tracks experiments, registers models and serves them. Feast serves features from Iceberg tables and Valkey, and Evidently stores drift reports. The Airflow image has the MLflow and Feast clients, with the tracking URI and the Feast registry already set.
  • AI. PostgreSQL has pgvector and pg_textsearch for hybrid search, and Valkey has vector search. An AI assistant can choose a profile and reach its services with the odctl skill and llms.txt, as Getting started describes. The Roadmap adds an MCP server for AI agents, a Langfuse profile for tracing LLM and agent applications, and a desflow server profile after desflow 1.0.

docs.title: Airflow DAGs from S3
docs.text:
The airflow profile runs airflow standalone in one container against odctl's PostgreSQL. It reads DAG files from s3://airflow/dags on SeaweedFS, so you deploy a DAG by uploading it. No volume or sync container is involved. The end-to-end tests run the steps below on every release.

This guide builds on Getting Started. Look at the left of the diagram: DAG files go to SeaweedFS, and Airflow reads them from there.

Start the profile:

docs/snippets/airflow-dags/commands.sh:up
odctl up airflow
Endpoint Address Web UI and REST API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8085, user user, password password Web UI and REST API inside the odctl network http://airflow:8080 DAG folder s3://airflow/dags on SeaweedFS

docs.title: Upload a DAG
docs.text:
Any S3 client pointed at http://127.0.0.1:8333 with key user and secret password can upload. This uses boto3 inside the Airflow container to write the DAG hello, with one task that runs echo hello:

docs/snippets/airflow-dags/commands.sh:upload
docker exec -i airflow python - <<'PY'
import boto3
body = '''
from airflow.sdk import DAG
from airflow.providers.standard.operators.bash import BashOperator
import pendulum

with DAG(
    dag_id="hello",
    start_date=pendulum.datetime(2026, 1, 1, tz="UTC"),
    schedule=None,
    catchup=False,
):
    BashOperator(task_id="say_hello", bash_command="echo hello")
'''
boto3.client("s3", endpoint_url="http://seaweed:8333").put_object(
    Bucket="airflow", Key="dags/hello.py", Body=body.encode())
PY

The upload prints nothing. Airflow checks the bucket every 15 seconds and then parses the new file. The interval is set today by refresh_interval in AIRFLOW__DAG_PROCESSOR__DAG_BUNDLE_CONFIG_LIST in .odctl/compose-orch.yml, where an edit can change it.

docs.title: Run It
docs.text:
New DAGs start paused. Wait until the DAG is listed, then unpause it, trigger it and list its runs:

docs/snippets/airflow-dags/commands.sh:run
docker exec airflow airflow dags list | grep hello
docker exec airflow airflow dags unpause hello
docker exec airflow airflow dags trigger hello
docker exec airflow airflow dags list-runs hello

The first command prints the hello line of the list. The last lists the run with its run_id, such as manual__2026-10-24T04:55:03.340843+00:00, in state queued or running, and listing it again a few seconds later shows success. The DAG page shows the run and the say_hello task.

docs.title: Plugins and Packages
docs.text:
Plugins are copied from s3://airflow/plugins when the container starts, because Airflow loads plugins only once. Run odctl restart airflow after changing one.

Tasks already have the MLflow and Feast clients, and MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI points at the mlflow profile. How It Works shows how to install extra Python packages with _AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, the Airflow API is http://airflow:8080, and tasks reach SeaweedFS at http://seaweed:8333 and MLflow at http://mlflow:5000.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It runs the steps above and waits for each one:

docs/snippets/airflow-dags/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts airflow, uploads a DAG to s3://airflow/dags, waits until Airflow has
# parsed it, triggers a run and waits until the run finishes.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up airflow

docker exec -i airflow python - <<'PY'
import boto3
body = '''
from airflow.sdk import DAG
from airflow.providers.standard.operators.bash import BashOperator
import pendulum

with DAG(
    dag_id="hello",
    start_date=pendulum.datetime(2026, 1, 1, tz="UTC"),
    schedule=None,
    catchup=False,
):
    BashOperator(task_id="say_hello", bash_command="echo hello")
'''
boto3.client("s3", endpoint_url="http://seaweed:8333").put_object(
    Bucket="airflow", Key="dags/hello.py", Body=body.encode())
PY

# Airflow checks the bucket every 15 seconds, then parses the new file.
until docker exec airflow airflow dags list 2>/dev/null | grep hello >/dev/null; do sleep 5; done
docker exec airflow airflow dags unpause hello
docker exec airflow airflow dags trigger hello >/dev/null

until docker exec airflow airflow dags list-runs hello -o plain 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'success|failed' >/dev/null; do sleep 5; done
docker exec airflow airflow dags list-runs hello -o plain

It prints the hello line from airflow dags unpause and then the run, in state success.

docs.title: ClickHouse
docs.text:
ClickHouse is a column-oriented database for analytical queries. A shard holds part of a table's rows, and each replica of a shard holds a copy of that part. ClickHouse Keeper is the coordination service that keeps the replicas of a shard in step. The ch-lite profile runs one shard with two replicas, ch-11 and ch-12, coordinated by ClickHouse Keeper in ch-keeper. ch-full adds a second shard, ch-21 and ch-22. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on Getting Started. Start the profile:

docs/snippets/clickhouse/commands.sh:up
odctl up ch-lite
Endpoint Address HTTP from the host http://127.0.0.1:8123 (ch-11) and http://127.0.0.1:8124 (ch-12); ch-full adds 8125 (ch-21) and 8126 (ch-22) Native protocol from the host 127.0.0.1:9000 (ch-11) and 127.0.0.1:9001 (ch-12); ch-full adds 9002 (ch-21) and 9003 (ch-22) Users default and user, both with the password password

Every server creates the feature_store and odctl databases when it starts with no data.

docs.title: Create a Table and Query It
docs.text:
clickhouse-client is in each server container. This lists the databases, then creates a table, writes 10 rows and counts them:

docs/snippets/clickhouse/commands.sh:merge-tree
docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q "SHOW DATABASES"

docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q \
  "CREATE TABLE default.demo (id UInt32) ENGINE=MergeTree ORDER BY id"
docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q \
  "INSERT INTO default.demo SELECT number FROM numbers(10)"
docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q \
  "SELECT count() FROM default.demo"

The first command lists default, feature_store, odctl and the system databases. The last prints 10.

ClickHouse also serves a query page at http://127.0.0.1:8123/play. Enter default and password in the top right, write a query and press Run.

docs.title: Replicate Across the Cluster
docs.text:
In ch-full, {cluster} names odctl_cluster, which has two shards of two replicas. A table created ON CLUSTER with ReplicatedMergeTree is created on all four servers, and Keeper keeps the two replicas of each shard in step:

docs/snippets/clickhouse/commands.sh:replicated
odctl up ch-full

docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q \
  "CREATE TABLE default.repl ON CLUSTER '{cluster}' (id UInt32) ENGINE=ReplicatedMergeTree ORDER BY id"
docker exec ch-11 clickhouse-client --password password -q \
  "INSERT INTO default.repl SELECT number FROM numbers(50)"

docker exec ch-12 clickhouse-client --password password -q "SELECT count() FROM default.repl"
docker exec ch-21 clickhouse-client --password password -q "SELECT count() FROM default.repl"

The CREATE prints one line for each of the four servers, with status 0 for success. ch-12, the other replica of shard 1, returns 50 once replication has caught up. ch-21 returns 0, because shard 2 holds only the rows written to it.

In ch-lite, {cluster} names odctl_single_shard, which holds ch-11 and ch-12 only, so ON CLUSTER statements finish without waiting for the missing shard.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, connect to ch-11:8123 over HTTP or ch-11:9000 with the native protocol, with the same users. Trino's clickhouse catalog reads the feature_store database on ch-11, as Trino and Metabase shows.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It runs on ch-lite, where {cluster} holds the two replicas of one shard, and uses tables of its own for each run:

docs/snippets/clickhouse/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts ch-lite, writes 10 rows to a MergeTree table and 50 rows to a
# replicated table, and counts the replicated rows on the other replica.
# Each run uses its own table names.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up ch-lite

run=$(date +%s)
ch() { docker exec "$1" clickhouse-client --password password -q "$2"; }

ch ch-11 "CREATE TABLE default.demo_$run (id UInt32) ENGINE=MergeTree ORDER BY id"
ch ch-11 "INSERT INTO default.demo_$run SELECT number FROM numbers(10)"
ch ch-11 "SELECT count() FROM default.demo_$run"

ch ch-11 "CREATE TABLE default.repl_$run ON CLUSTER '{cluster}' (id UInt32) ENGINE=ReplicatedMergeTree ORDER BY id" >/dev/null
ch ch-11 "INSERT INTO default.repl_$run SELECT number FROM numbers(50)"
# ch-12 is the other replica of the same shard; replication takes a moment.
until [ "$(ch ch-12 "SELECT count() FROM default.repl_$run")" = "50" ]; do sleep 1; done
echo "ch-12 holds 50 rows of repl_$run"

It prints 10, then ch-12 holds 50 rows of with the replicated table's name.

docs.title: Evidently Reports
docs.text:
The evidently profile runs the Evidently UI and API. Evidently checks data drift and data quality. Data drift is a change in the distribution of a column between a reference dataset and current data. Your client computes each report and pushes the result to the server. The server keeps projects, reports, dashboards and datasets in the evidently database on PostgreSQL. The end-to-end tests run the code below on every release.

This guide builds on Getting Started.

Endpoint Address UI and API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8089 API inside the odctl network http://evidently:8000

Start the profile and install the client:

docs/snippets/evidently-reports/commands.sh:install
odctl up evidently
pip install evidently==0.7.23 "pandas<3.1"

The server runs Evidently 0.7.23, so install the same client version. Evidently 0.7.23 fails to import with pandas 3.1, so keep pandas below 3.1. The UI has no login.

docs.title: Push a Data Drift Report
docs.text:
This creates the project demo, builds a reference dataset and a current one, computes a data drift report and pushes it to the server:

docs/snippets/evidently-reports/steps.py:report
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from evidently import Report
from evidently.presets import DataDriftPreset
from evidently.ui.workspace import RemoteWorkspace

ws = RemoteWorkspace("http://127.0.0.1:8089")
project = ws.create_project("demo")

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
reference = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.normal(0, 1, 500), "y": rng.normal(0, 1, 500)})
current = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.normal(3, 1, 500), "y": rng.normal(0, 1, 500)})

snapshot = Report([DataDriftPreset()]).run(current_data=current, reference_data=reference)
ws.add_run(project.id, snapshot)

The code prints nothing. Column x moves by three standard deviations and y does not, so the report in the UI shows one drifted column.

Open the report under the project's Reports tab:

docs.title: Store a Dataset
docs.text:
This stores a small table as a dataset in the same project and reads it back:

docs/snippets/evidently-reports/steps.py:dataset
from evidently import DataDefinition, Dataset

data = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "score": [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]})
dataset_id = ws.add_dataset(project.id, Dataset.from_pandas(data, data_definition=DataDefinition()), "demo")
print(ws.load_dataset(dataset_id).as_dataframe())

It prints the dataset read back from the server, with the columns id and score and three rows. The dataset is stored in the evidently database, with the projects and reports.

docs.title: Performance Without Outcomes
docs.text: Evidently gives no estimate of a model's performance while the outcomes are unknown. NannyML gives one. NannyML 0.13.1 supports Python 3.9 to 3.12, and the Airflow image runs Python 3.13. Run NannyML in a Python 3.12 process on your machine instead.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, connect with RemoteWorkspace("http://evidently:8000"). For Airflow tasks, set _AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS="evidently==0.7.23" in .odctl/.env and run odctl recreate airflow. The server's settings are in evidently/config.yaml in the workspace.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.py. Start the profile and install the client as above, then run it with python example.py. It creates the project demo-example:

docs/snippets/evidently-reports/example.py
"""Pushes a data drift report to Evidently, stores a dataset and reads it back.

Start the profile with `odctl up evidently` and install the client with
`pip install evidently==0.7.23 "pandas<3.1"` first.
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from evidently import DataDefinition, Dataset, Report
from evidently.presets import DataDriftPreset
from evidently.ui.workspace import RemoteWorkspace

ws = RemoteWorkspace("http://127.0.0.1:8089")
project = ws.create_project("demo-example")

# Column x moves by three standard deviations and y does not.
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
reference = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.normal(0, 1, 500), "y": rng.normal(0, 1, 500)})
current = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.normal(3, 1, 500), "y": rng.normal(0, 1, 500)})
snapshot = Report([DataDriftPreset()]).run(current_data=current, reference_data=reference)
ws.add_run(project.id, snapshot)
print(f"report pushed to project {project.id}")

data = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "score": [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]})
dataset = Dataset.from_pandas(data, data_definition=DataDefinition())
dataset_id = ws.add_dataset(project.id, dataset, "demo")
print(ws.load_dataset(dataset_id).as_dataframe())

It prints report pushed to project with the project's id, and then the dataset with its three rows.

docs.title: Feast with Iceberg
docs.text:
Feast is a feature store: it keeps the definitions of a model's input features and serves their values. The offline store holds the history of each feature, for training. The online store holds each entity's latest value, for serving a prediction quickly. Materialising copies values from the offline store to the online store. The feast profile runs the Feast UI and the online feature server. Feast stores no feature values of its own. Feature definitions live in a SQL registry in PostgreSQL, offline values come from Iceberg tables through the REST catalog, and online values are served from Valkey. You run feast apply and the other client commands from your own environment. The end-to-end tests run the steps below on every release.

This guide builds on Ingest into Iceberg, which writes Iceberg tables through the catalog, and Flink SQL, whose SQL client the last step uses. Follow the arrows from the feast CLI on the left: definitions go to the registry, and values go from Iceberg to Valkey.

Start the profile and install the client, with the extras that read Iceberg, PostgreSQL and Valkey:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/commands.sh:install
odctl up feast
pip install "feast[duckdb,iceberg,redis,postgres]==0.66.0" pyarrow
Endpoint Address Feast UI http://127.0.0.1:8890 Feature server from the host http://127.0.0.1:6566 Feature server inside the odctl network http://feast-serve:6566 Registry the feast database on PostgreSQL

docs.title: Point the Clients at the Stack
docs.text:
PyIceberg, which Feast uses to read Iceberg, takes its catalog settings from the environment. Run these in the shell where you run the next steps:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/commands.sh:catalog-env
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__TYPE=rest
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__URI=http://127.0.0.1:8181
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__WAREHOUSE=s3://warehouse/
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__S3__ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:8333
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__S3__ACCESS_KEY_ID=user
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__S3__SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=password
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__S3__PATH_STYLE_ACCESS=true
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__ODCTL__S3__REGION=us-east-1

docs.title: Create an Iceberg Table
docs.text:
Save this code as create_table.py and run it with python create_table.py. It creates demo.driver_stats and writes one hour-old row for each of two drivers:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/steps.py:create-table
import datetime, pyarrow as pa
from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog

cat = load_catalog("odctl")
cat.create_namespace_if_not_exists("demo")
schema = pa.schema([
    pa.field("driver_id", pa.int64(), nullable=False),
    pa.field("event_timestamp", pa.timestamp("us", tz="UTC"), nullable=False),
    pa.field("conv_rate", pa.float32(), nullable=False),
])
t = cat.create_table("demo.driver_stats", schema=schema)
now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0)
t.append(pa.Table.from_pydict({
    "driver_id": [1001, 1002],
    "event_timestamp": [now - datetime.timedelta(hours=1)] * 2,
    "conv_rate": [0.5, 0.75],
}, schema=schema))

docs.title: Define the Feature Repository
docs.text:
A feature repository is a folder of configuration and definitions. Save this file as feature_repo/feature_store.yaml. It names the registry, the offline store and the online store:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/feature_repo/feature_store.yaml
project: demo
provider: local
registry:
  registry_type: sql
  path: postgresql+psycopg://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/feast
offline_store:
  type: duckdb
online_store:
  type: redis
  connection_string: "127.0.0.1:6379,username=user,password=password"
entity_key_serialization_version: 3

Save the definitions as feature_repo/definitions.py. They declare the entity driver and the feature view driver_stats over the Iceberg table:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/feature_repo/definitions.py
from datetime import timedelta
from feast import Entity, FeatureView, Field
from feast.types import Float32
from feast.infra.data_sources.contrib.iceberg_catalog.iceberg_source import IcebergSource

driver = Entity(name="driver", join_keys=["driver_id"])
src = IcebergSource(
    warehouse="", namespace="demo", table="driver_stats",
    catalog_type="rest", catalog_name="odctl",
    endpoint="http://127.0.0.1:8181",
    timestamp_field="event_timestamp",
)
fv = FeatureView(
    name="driver_stats", entities=[driver], ttl=timedelta(days=365),
    schema=[Field(name="conv_rate", dtype=Float32)], source=src, online=True,
)

Pass warehouse="" and catalog_name="odctl". Feast's REST client puts the warehouse into the URL path, and the catalog serves its API with no prefix, so a real warehouse value fails with HTTP 400.

docs.title: Register and Materialise
docs.text:
Run these from the folder that holds feature_repo. apply writes the definitions to the registry, and materialize-incremental copies the latest values into Valkey:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/commands.sh:apply-materialize
feast -c feature_repo apply
feast -c feature_repo materialize-incremental "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S)"

apply prints Applying changes for project demo and Deploying infrastructure for driver_stats, and materialize-incremental names the feature view and the time range it copied.

docs.title: Read the Features
docs.text:
FeatureStore(repo_path="feature_repo").get_historical_features(...) takes a point-in-time join from Iceberg through DuckDB, for training. This reads the materialised values from Valkey instead, as a model server would:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/steps.py:read
from feast import FeatureStore

fs = FeatureStore(repo_path="feature_repo")
print(fs.get_online_features(
    features=["driver_stats:conv_rate"],
    entity_rows=[{"driver_id": 1001}, {"driver_id": 1002}],
).to_dict())

It prints {'driver_id': [1001, 1002], 'conv_rate': [0.5, 0.75]}.

docs.title: Serve from the Stack
docs.text:
The UI at http://127.0.0.1:8890 and the online feature server at http://127.0.0.1:6566 load their repository from s3://feast/repo. To serve your features, upload the repository there with container addresses in its feature_store.yaml: postgres:5432, valkey:6379 and http://catalog:8181. The services check that prefix every 15 seconds and restart Feast when it changes. The interval is set today by time.sleep(15) in x-feast-repo-sync in .odctl/compose-mlops.yml.

Once the repository is uploaded, the UI lists the project and its feature views:

docs.title: Push Features from Flink SQL
docs.text:
A push source lets a client write a feature value straight to the online store, through the feature server's /push endpoint, instead of materialising it. Flink's HTTP connector sends rows to a URL, so a Flink SQL job can push each value it computes. Start Flink beside Feast:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/commands.sh:up
odctl up flink-lite

Feast needs a push source before it accepts a push, and the feature server reads its own repository, so the definitions go into the feast-serve container. Save these definitions as push_definitions.py. They declare the push source driver_push and the feature view driver_pushed:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/push_definitions.py
from datetime import timedelta
from feast import Entity, FeatureView, Field, FileSource, PushSource
from feast.types import Float32, Int64
from feast.value_type import ValueType

driver = Entity(name="driver", join_keys=["driver_id"], value_type=ValueType.INT64)
# Nothing reads this file. A push source needs a batch source behind it.
batch = FileSource(path="/tmp/driver_stats.parquet", timestamp_field="event_timestamp")
push = PushSource(name="driver_push", batch_source=batch)
driver_pushed = FeatureView(
    name="driver_pushed",
    entities=[driver],
    ttl=timedelta(days=1),
    schema=[Field(name="driver_id", dtype=Int64), Field(name="conv_rate", dtype=Float32)],
    source=push,
    online=True,
)

Copy the definitions into the Feast container and apply them. --skip-source-validation stops Feast from looking for the file behind the batch source:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/commands.sh:push-apply
docker cp push_definitions.py feast-serve:/tmp/feature_repo/push_definitions.py
docker exec feast-serve feast -c /tmp/feature_repo apply --skip-source-validation

apply prints Applying changes for project odctl and Deploying infrastructure for driver_pushed. Open the SQL client:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/commands.sh:sql-client
docker exec -it flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh

Then run these statements, which push the value 0.9 for driver 1001:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/steps.sql:feast-push
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE feast_push (
  push_source_name STRING,
  df ROW<driver_id ARRAY<BIGINT>, conv_rate ARRAY<DOUBLE>, event_timestamp ARRAY<TIMESTAMP_LTZ(3)>>,
  allow_registry_cache BOOLEAN
) WITH (
  'connector' = 'http-async-sink',
  'url' = 'http://feast-serve:6566/push',
  'format' = 'json',
  'http.sink.writer.request.mode' = 'single',
  'http.sink.header.Content-Type' = 'application/json'
);
INSERT INTO feast_push SELECT 'driver_push', ROW(ARRAY[CAST(1001 AS BIGINT)], ARRAY[CAST(0.9 AS DOUBLE)], ARRAY[CURRENT_TIMESTAMP]), FALSE;

The connector is http-async-sink. Its default sends rows in batches as one JSON array. Feast's /push takes one JSON object, so http.sink.writer.request.mode is single, which sends one request for each row. The sink sends no Content-Type header, and Feast answers 422 without one, so http.sink.header.Content-Type sets it. The column names are the field names of the request body. Feast reads df as a table of columns, so each field holds an array.

Feast caches its registry for up to a minute after apply. allow_registry_cache set to FALSE makes the push read the registry again, so it works at once. The timestamp must be new: a push with the same event_timestamp as the stored value does not replace it, so the statement uses CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.

The Flink job finishes and prints Complete execution of the SQL update statement. even when Feast rejects the request. The failure is only in the TaskManager log as Http Sink failed to write. Read the value back from Feast to check the push:

docs/snippets/feast-iceberg/commands.sh:push-read
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6566/get-online-features \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"features": ["driver_pushed:conv_rate"], "entities": {"driver_id": [1001]}}'

The answer holds 0.8999999761581421 for conv_rate, which is 0.9 as a 32-bit float. The read also uses the cached registry, so right after apply it can answer that the feature view does not exist. Run it again after a minute.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, the feature server is http://feast-serve:6566. A repository for the services uses postgres:5432 for the registry, valkey:6379 for the online store and http://catalog:8181 for Iceberg.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace, in an environment with the client installed as above. It writes the repository files into feature_repo in that folder, and appends two rows to demo.driver_stats on each run:

    | grep 0.8999999761581421; do
  sleep 5
done

It prints {'driver_id': [1001, 1002], 'conv_rate': [0.5, 0.75]} and then the feature server's answer with 0.8999999761581421.

docs.title: Flink SQL: Kafka to PostgreSQL
docs.text:
The flink-lite profile runs a Flink JobManager, one TaskManager and the SQL Gateway. flink-full runs three TaskManagers. Flink's connector jars for Kafka, Avro with the schema registry, JDBC, Iceberg and HTTP come from the shared volume that the deps profile fills. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide reads Avro records from Kafka through the Karapace schema registry and writes an aggregate to PostgreSQL over JDBC. It builds on Kafka, which starts kafka-lite and creates a topic. Ingest into Iceberg shows Flink writing an Iceberg table, Rolling Windows computes features over several window sizes, and Feast with Iceberg sends rows to Feast over HTTP.

Follow the arrows from the TaskManager: it writes Avro records to the orders topic, reads them back and writes the totals to PostgreSQL.

Start both profiles:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/commands.sh:up
odctl up flink-lite kafka-lite

flink-lite starts PostgreSQL itself, because it depends on the Iceberg catalog, which keeps its metadata there.

Endpoint Address Flink UI and REST API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8082 SQL Gateway REST API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8084 Flink REST API inside the odctl network http://jobmanager:8081 SQL Gateway inside the odctl network http://flink-sql-gateway:8083

docs.title: Create the Topic and the Target Table
docs.text:
This creates the Kafka topic orders and the PostgreSQL table supplier_stats that the job writes to:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/commands.sh:create-topic-table
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --if-not-exists --topic orders --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1

docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  CREATE TABLE supplier_stats (supplier TEXT PRIMARY KEY, orders BIGINT, total DOUBLE PRECISION);"

The commands print Created topic orders. and CREATE TABLE.

docs.title: Run the SQL
docs.text:
Open the SQL client in the JobManager container:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/commands.sh:sql-client
docker exec -it flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh

Run these statements in the client. They declare the topic and the PostgreSQL table as Flink tables, write three orders and sum them by supplier:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/steps.sql:kafka-to-postgres
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE orders (supplier STRING, price DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='kafka','topic'='orders','properties.bootstrap.servers'='broker-1:19092','scan.startup.mode'='earliest-offset','scan.bounded.mode'='latest-offset','format'='avro-confluent','avro-confluent.url'='http://karapace:8081');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES ('a', 10.0), ('a', 5.0), ('b', 7.5);
CREATE TABLE stats (supplier STRING, orders BIGINT, total DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY (supplier) NOT ENFORCED) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='supplier_stats','username'='user','password'='password');
INSERT INTO stats SELECT supplier, COUNT(*), SUM(price) FROM orders GROUP BY supplier;

Each statement prints [INFO] Execute statement succeeded. or, for an INSERT, [INFO] Complete execution of the SQL update statement. The first INSERT writes three Avro records to Kafka and registers their schema in Karapace. The second reads them back, groups them by supplier and writes the result to PostgreSQL. scan.bounded.mode set to latest-offset makes the Kafka source stop at the end of the topic, so the batch job finishes. Leave it out and set execution.runtime-mode to streaming for a job that keeps running.

Right after Kafka starts, Karapace can answer its health check and still time out on a schema write for a short while. If the first INSERT fails on the schema registry, run it again.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
This reads the table the job wrote:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/commands.sh:check
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "SELECT * FROM supplier_stats ORDER BY supplier"

Supplier a has 2 orders totalling 15, and supplier b has 1 order totalling 7.5:

 supplier | orders | total
----------+--------+-------
 a        |      2 |    15
 b        |      1 |   7.5
(2 rows)

The Flink UI at http://127.0.0.1:8082 shows the jobs the SQL client submitted.

The two INSERT statements run as two batch jobs, listed under Completed Jobs.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, Flink's REST API is http://jobmanager:8081 and the SQL Gateway is http://flink-sql-gateway:8083. In Flink SQL, Kafka is broker-1:19092, Karapace is http://karapace:8081 and PostgreSQL is jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It runs the steps above with a topic and a table of its own for each run, so it can run again:

docs/snippets/flink-sql/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts flink-lite and kafka-lite, writes three Avro records to a Kafka topic
# with Flink SQL, sums them by supplier into PostgreSQL and prints the result.
# Each run uses its own topic and table names, so the file can run again.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up flink-lite kafka-lite

# Karapace answers its health check before it can store a schema, so wait
# until it accepts one.
until curl -fs -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json' \
  -d '{"schema": "{\"type\": \"string\"}"}' http://127.0.0.1:8081/subjects/ready/versions >/dev/null; do
  sleep 5
done

run=$(date +%s)
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --topic "orders-$run" --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  CREATE TABLE supplier_stats_$run (supplier TEXT PRIMARY KEY, orders BIGINT, total DOUBLE PRECISION);"

docker exec -i flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh <<SQL | grep -E 'ERROR|Exception' || true
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE orders (supplier STRING, price DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='kafka','topic'='orders-$run','properties.bootstrap.servers'='broker-1:19092','scan.startup.mode'='earliest-offset','scan.bounded.mode'='latest-offset','format'='avro-confluent','avro-confluent.url'='http://karapace:8081');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES ('a', 10.0), ('a', 5.0), ('b', 7.5);
CREATE TABLE stats (supplier STRING, orders BIGINT, total DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY (supplier) NOT ENFORCED) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='supplier_stats_$run','username'='user','password'='password');
INSERT INTO stats SELECT supplier, COUNT(*), SUM(price) FROM orders GROUP BY supplier;
SQL

docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "SELECT * FROM supplier_stats_$run ORDER BY supplier"

It prints the same two rows as Check the Result: a with 2 orders totalling 15, and b with 1 order totalling 7.5.

docs.title: Fluss
docs.text:
Apache Fluss is a streaming storage for real-time analytics: it keeps tables that Flink writes and reads with low latency, either as logs or as tables with a primary key. The fluss profile runs a coordinator server, one tablet server and the ZooKeeper they register in. Flink reads and writes Fluss tables through the Fluss catalog, whose client jar comes from the shared volume that the deps profile fills. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on Flink SQL, which opens the SQL client. Start both profiles:

docs/snippets/fluss/commands.sh:up
odctl up fluss flink-lite
Endpoint Address Coordinator inside the odctl network fluss-coordinator:9123 Tablet server inside the odctl network fluss-tablet-1:9123

The coordinator is also published on 127.0.0.1:9123 and the tablet server on 127.0.0.1:9124. Both advertise their container names, which resolve only inside the odctl network, so run Fluss clients in a container, such as Flink.

docs.title: Check the Cluster Formed
docs.text:
The servers register in ZooKeeper once they are up. This lists the tablet servers and reads the active coordinator:

docs/snippets/fluss/commands.sh:registrations
docker exec fluss-zookeeper zkCli.sh -server localhost:2181 ls /fluss/tabletservers/ids
docker exec fluss-zookeeper zkCli.sh -server localhost:2181 get /fluss/coordinators/active

Among the ZooKeeper client's log lines, the first command prints [0], the id of the one tablet server. The second prints a JSON object whose listeners include CLIENT://fluss-coordinator:9123.

docs.title: Write and Read a Table with Flink SQL
docs.text:
Open the SQL client in the JobManager container:

docs/snippets/fluss/commands.sh:sql-client
docker exec -it flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh

Run these statements in the client. They register the Fluss catalog, create a table with a primary key, write three rows and read them back:

docs/snippets/fluss/steps.sql:table
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
SET 'sql-client.execution.result-mode' = 'tableau';
CREATE CATALOG fluss_catalog WITH ('type' = 'fluss', 'bootstrap.servers' = 'fluss-coordinator:9123');
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS fluss_catalog.demo;
CREATE TABLE fluss_catalog.demo.t (id BIGINT, name STRING, PRIMARY KEY (id) NOT ENFORCED);
INSERT INTO fluss_catalog.demo.t VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'c');
SELECT * FROM fluss_catalog.demo.t LIMIT 10;

The SELECT returns the three rows:

| id | name |
+----+------+
|  1 |    a |
|  2 |    b |
|  3 |    c |
+----+------+

Fluss keeps its data inside its containers, so odctl down removes it.

The Flink UI lists the two jobs:

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, set a Fluss client's bootstrap servers to fluss-coordinator:9123.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It waits until the tablet server has registered, then runs the SQL above with a table of its own for each run:

docs/snippets/fluss/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts fluss and flink-lite, then writes three rows to a Fluss table with
# Flink SQL and reads them back. Each run uses its own table name.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up fluss flink-lite

# The tablet server registers in ZooKeeper a few seconds after it starts.
until docker exec fluss-zookeeper zkCli.sh -server localhost:2181 ls /fluss/tabletservers/ids 2>/dev/null | grep '^\[0' >/dev/null; do
  sleep 2
done

run=$(date +%s)
docker exec -i flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh <<SQL | grep -E '^[|+]|ERROR'
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
SET 'sql-client.execution.result-mode' = 'tableau';
CREATE CATALOG fluss_catalog WITH ('type' = 'fluss', 'bootstrap.servers' = 'fluss-coordinator:9123');
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS fluss_catalog.demo;
CREATE TABLE fluss_catalog.demo.t_$run (id BIGINT, name STRING, PRIMARY KEY (id) NOT ENFORCED);
INSERT INTO fluss_catalog.demo.t_$run VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'c');
SELECT * FROM fluss_catalog.demo.t_$run LIMIT 10;
SQL

It prints the same three rows as the SELECT above.

docs.title: Hybrid Search in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
odctl's PostgreSQL image adds pgvector for vector search and pg_textsearch for BM25 keyword ranking. Vector search finds the rows whose embeddings are nearest to a query embedding. BM25 is a ranking function that scores a text by how often it holds the query's words, weighted by how rare each word is. Both extensions are created in the vector database. Hybrid search runs both queries and combines their rankings, which your application or a final SQL query does. The end-to-end tests run the SQL below on every release.

This guide builds on Getting Started.

Endpoint Address PostgreSQL from the host 127.0.0.1:5432, user user, password password PostgreSQL inside the odctl network postgres:5432 Database with both extensions vector

Start the profile and open psql in the container:

docs/snippets/hybrid-search/commands.sh:psql
odctl up postgres
docker exec -it postgres psql -U user -d vector

docs.title: Vector Similarity with pgvector
docs.text:
This creates a table of three-dimensional vectors with an HNSW index and returns the row nearest to [1,0,0]:

docs/snippets/hybrid-search/steps.sql:vector
CREATE TABLE items (id bigserial primary key, embedding vector(3));
INSERT INTO items (embedding) VALUES ('[1,0,0]'), ('[0,1,0]'), ('[0.9,0.1,0]');
CREATE INDEX items_hnsw ON items USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops);

SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> '[1,0,0]' LIMIT 1;

<-> is the Euclidean distance, so the nearest row comes first, and the query returns id 1. The index is an HNSW index: HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world) is a graph of the vectors in layers, which finds near neighbours without comparing the query with every row.

docs.title: Keyword Ranking with pg_textsearch
docs.text:
This creates a table of three texts with a BM25 index and returns the best match for ranking function:

docs/snippets/hybrid-search/steps.sql:bm25
CREATE TABLE docs (id int primary key, content text);
INSERT INTO docs VALUES
  (1, 'PostgreSQL is a powerful database system'),
  (2, 'BM25 is an effective ranking function'),
  (3, 'Full text search with custom scoring');
CREATE INDEX docs_bm25 ON docs USING bm25(content) WITH (text_config='english');

SELECT id FROM docs ORDER BY content <@> 'ranking function' LIMIT 1;

Ordering by content <@> 'query' puts the best BM25 match first, so the query returns id 2. pg_textsearch works only when PostgreSQL preloads it, and odctl's compose file sets shared_preload_libraries to do that.

psql shows each query's result:

To use the extensions in another database, run CREATE EXTENSION vector; or CREATE EXTENSION pg_textsearch; there.

docs.title: From Another Container
