docs.text: Inside the odctl network, connect to postgres:5432 with the same user and password, for example postgresql://user:password@postgres:5432/vector.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It runs both queries on tables named demo_items and demo_docs, which it drops and creates again on every run:

docs/snippets/hybrid-search/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts postgres and runs a vector query and a BM25 query in the vector
# database, on tables it creates again on every run.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up postgres

docker exec -i postgres psql -U user -d vector -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 <<'SQL'
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS demo_items, demo_docs;

CREATE TABLE demo_items (id bigserial primary key, embedding vector(3));
INSERT INTO demo_items (embedding) VALUES ('[1,0,0]'), ('[0,1,0]'), ('[0.9,0.1,0]');
CREATE INDEX demo_items_hnsw ON demo_items USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops);
SELECT id FROM demo_items ORDER BY embedding <-> '[1,0,0]' LIMIT 1;

CREATE TABLE demo_docs (id int primary key, content text);
INSERT INTO demo_docs VALUES
  (1, 'PostgreSQL is a powerful database system'),
  (2, 'BM25 is an effective ranking function'),
  (3, 'Full text search with custom scoring');
CREATE INDEX demo_docs_bm25 ON demo_docs USING bm25(content) WITH (text_config='english');
SELECT id FROM demo_docs ORDER BY content <@> 'ranking function' LIMIT 1;
SQL

It prints the statements' results, with id 1 from the vector query and id 2 from the BM25 query. The BM25 index build also prints NOTICE lines.

docs.title: Ingest into Iceberg
docs.text:
Kafka Connect, Flink and Spark all write Iceberg tables through the same REST catalog, http://catalog:8181, with the files on SeaweedFS under s3://warehouse. SeaweedFS is an object store with an S3 API, which odctl's storage profile runs. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on Kafka Connect, which registers a connector, and Flink SQL, which runs statements in the SQL client.

kafka-lite does not start the catalog, so start both:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/commands.sh:up
odctl up kafka-lite catalog
Endpoint Address Catalog REST API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8181 Catalog REST API inside the odctl network http://catalog:8181 SeaweedFS S3 API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8333 SeaweedFS S3 API inside the odctl network http://seaweed:8333 SeaweedFS file browser http://127.0.0.1:8889

docs.title: Kafka Connect Sink
docs.text:
The Iceberg sink in Kafka Connect reads a topic and commits its records to an Iceberg table through the catalog. Look at the sink in the middle: it writes data files to SeaweedFS and commits each batch through the catalog, which keeps its tables in PostgreSQL.

The sink writes to a table that exists. This creates the namespace demo and the table kc through the catalog's REST API:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/commands.sh:create-table
api=http://127.0.0.1:8181/v1/namespaces
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"namespace":["demo"]}' "$api"
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"kc","schema":{"type":"struct","schema-id":0,"fields":[{"id":1,"name":"id","required":false,"type":"long"},{"id":2,"name":"name","required":false,"type":"string"}]}}' \
  "$api/demo/tables"

Each call answers with the namespace or the table's metadata as JSON. The sink also needs its topic and a control topic, where its tasks agree on each commit. This creates both and writes five JSON records:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/commands.sh:topics-produce
for topic in demo-iceberg control-iceberg; do
  docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
    --create --if-not-exists --topic "$topic" --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
done
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo "{\"id\":$i,\"name\":\"n$i\"}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic demo-iceberg

Save the sink's configuration as demo-iceberg.json. It reads plain JSON, so it sets "value.converter.schemas.enable": "false" instead of the worker's default:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/demo-iceberg.json
{
  "name": "demo-iceberg",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "org.apache.iceberg.connect.IcebergSinkConnector",
    "tasks.max": "1",
    "topics": "demo-iceberg",
    "value.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.json.JsonConverter",
    "value.converter.schemas.enable": "false",
    "key.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.StringConverter",
    "iceberg.tables": "demo.kc",
    "iceberg.control.commit.interval-ms": "10000",
    "iceberg.kafka.session.timeout.ms": "300000",
    "iceberg.kafka.heartbeat.interval.ms": "3000",
    "iceberg.kafka.auto.offset.reset": "earliest",
    "consumer.override.auto.offset.reset": "earliest",
    "iceberg.catalog.type": "rest",
    "iceberg.catalog.uri": "http://catalog:8181",
    "iceberg.catalog.io-impl": "org.apache.iceberg.aws.s3.S3FileIO",
    "iceberg.catalog.client.region": "us-east-1",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.endpoint": "http://seaweed:8333",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.path-style-access": "true",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.access-key-id": "user",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.secret-access-key": "password"
  }
}

Register it with Kafka Connect from the folder that holds the file:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/commands.sh:register
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors -d @demo-iceberg.json

The first commit can take a minute or more, because the sink waits for its control consumer to join a group. After that, the table's current snapshot counts the five records:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/commands.sh:records
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8181/v1/namespaces/demo/tables/kc | grep -o '"total-records":"[0-9]*"'

The command prints "total-records":"5". Then check the connector and remove it:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/commands.sh:status-remove
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-iceberg/status
curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-iceberg

The status shows "state":"RUNNING" for the connector and its task. Kafka UI lists the sink under Kafka Connect, Connectors while it is registered:

The table's data and metadata files are in SeaweedFS, whose browser at http://127.0.0.1:8889 lists the buckets, including warehouse.

docs.title: Flink SQL
docs.text:
Start Flink and open its SQL client. flink-lite uses the catalog that is already running:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/commands.sh:flink-client
odctl up flink-lite
docker exec -it flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh

These statements register the catalog as ice, create a table, insert three rows and count them:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/steps.sql:flink
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
SET 'sql-client.execution.result-mode' = 'tableau';
CREATE CATALOG ice WITH ('type'='iceberg','catalog-type'='rest','uri'='http://catalog:8181','warehouse'='s3://warehouse','s3.endpoint'='http://seaweed:8333','s3.path-style-access'='true','s3.access-key-id'='user','s3.secret-access-key'='password');
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS ice.demo_flink;
CREATE TABLE ice.demo_flink.t (id BIGINT, name STRING);
INSERT INTO ice.demo_flink.t VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'c');
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ice.demo_flink.t;

The SELECT prints 3.

docs.title: Spark SQL
docs.text:
Spark's default catalog already points at the same REST catalog, as Spark shows when it creates and queries a table.

Every engine sees the same tables, so a table written by one can be read by the others, and by Trino through its iceberg catalog.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, an Iceberg client uses the catalog at http://catalog:8181, the warehouse s3://warehouse, and SeaweedFS at http://seaweed:8333 with the key user and the secret password.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It runs the Kafka Connect sink and the Flink SQL steps above with names of its own for each run, so it can run again:

docs/snippets/iceberg-ingestion/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts kafka-lite and flink-lite, which starts the catalog, then writes five
# rows to an Iceberg table through the Kafka Connect sink and three rows to
# another through Flink SQL, and prints both counts. Each run uses its own
# topic, connector and table names, so the file can run again.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up kafka-lite flink-lite

run=$(date +%s)
api=http://127.0.0.1:8181/v1/namespaces
until curl -fs http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors >/dev/null; do sleep 2; done

# A namespace, which may exist already, and an empty table for the sink.
curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"namespace":["demo"]}' "$api"
curl -fs -o /dev/null -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"name\":\"kc_$run\",\"schema\":{\"type\":\"struct\",\"schema-id\":0,\"fields\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":\"id\",\"required\":false,\"type\":\"long\"},{\"id\":2,\"name\":\"name\",\"required\":false,\"type\":\"string\"}]}}" \
  "$api/demo/tables"

# Create the topic and the sink's control topic, then write five JSON records.
for topic in "iceberg-$run" "control-$run"; do
  docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
    --create --topic "$topic" --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
done
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo "{\"id\":$i,\"name\":\"n$i\"}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic "iceberg-$run"

curl -fs -o /dev/null -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors -d @- <<JSON
{
  "name": "iceberg-$run",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "org.apache.iceberg.connect.IcebergSinkConnector",
    "tasks.max": "1",
    "topics": "iceberg-$run",
    "value.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.json.JsonConverter",
    "value.converter.schemas.enable": "false",
    "key.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.StringConverter",
    "iceberg.tables": "demo.kc_$run",
    "iceberg.control.topic": "control-$run",
    "iceberg.control.commit.interval-ms": "10000",
    "iceberg.kafka.session.timeout.ms": "300000",
    "iceberg.kafka.heartbeat.interval.ms": "3000",
    "iceberg.kafka.auto.offset.reset": "earliest",
    "consumer.override.auto.offset.reset": "earliest",
    "iceberg.catalog.type": "rest",
    "iceberg.catalog.uri": "http://catalog:8181",
    "iceberg.catalog.io-impl": "org.apache.iceberg.aws.s3.S3FileIO",
    "iceberg.catalog.client.region": "us-east-1",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.endpoint": "http://seaweed:8333",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.path-style-access": "true",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.access-key-id": "user",
    "iceberg.catalog.s3.secret-access-key": "password"
  }
}
JSON

# The first commit can take a minute or more.
until curl -s "$api/demo/tables/kc_$run" | grep '"total-records":"5"' >/dev/null; do sleep 5; done
echo "demo.kc_$run: 5 records written by the Kafka Connect sink"
curl -s -o /dev/null -X DELETE "http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/iceberg-$run"

docker exec -i flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh <<SQL | grep -E '^[|+]'
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
SET 'sql-client.execution.result-mode' = 'tableau';
CREATE CATALOG ice WITH ('type'='iceberg','catalog-type'='rest','uri'='http://catalog:8181','warehouse'='s3://warehouse','s3.endpoint'='http://seaweed:8333','s3.path-style-access'='true','s3.access-key-id'='user','s3.secret-access-key'='password');
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS ice.demo_flink;
CREATE TABLE ice.demo_flink.t_$run (id BIGINT, name STRING);
INSERT INTO ice.demo_flink.t_$run VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'c');
SELECT COUNT(*) AS flink_rows FROM ice.demo_flink.t_$run;
SQL

It prints 5 records written by the Kafka Connect sink with the table's name, then a table with flink_rows equal to 3. The SQL client also prints warnings about the JVM and the terminal on its error output, which do not affect the result.

docs.title: Kafka Connect
docs.text:
Both Kafka profiles run one Kafka Connect worker, connect, beside the brokers. Kafka Connect runs connectors: a source connector writes records from another system into Kafka, and a sink connector writes records from Kafka into another system. The worker loads its connectors from the shared volume that the deps profile fills, and you manage them through its REST API. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on Kafka, which starts kafka-lite and reads a topic with the console consumer.

Start the profile:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:up
odctl up kafka-lite
Setting Value REST API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8083 REST API inside the odctl network http://connect:8083 Plugin folder /mnt/shared-deps/connect Default converters JSON with schemas, for keys and values Offset flush interval 10 seconds

The converters and the flush interval are set today in the connect service of .odctl/compose-kafka.yml (offset.flush.interval.ms=10000), where an edit can change them.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
The deps image puts these connectors in the plugin folder: the Apache Iceberg sink, the Debezium PostgreSQL source, the ClickHouse sink, the Aiven JDBC connector, the Aiven S3 sink, the Redis connector and the MSK data generator. This lists the classes Connect has loaded:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:plugins
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/connector-plugins

The reply is a JSON list with one entry per class. The tests check that it includes org.apache.iceberg.connect.IcebergSinkConnector, io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector and com.clickhouse.kafka.connect.ClickHouseSinkConnector. A plugin missing from the volume does not stop Connect from starting. It only leaves the class out of this list.

docs.title: Register a Connector
docs.text:
A connector is a name and a config object, posted to /connectors. The MSK data generator is a source connector that needs nothing but Kafka: it writes made-up records to a topic. Save this configuration as demo-datagen.json. It writes a record to the topic customers every half second, with an ISBN-10 number as its key, a first name and a number of visits from 1 to 10:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/demo-datagen.json
{
  "name": "demo-datagen",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "com.amazonaws.mskdatagen.GeneratorSourceConnector",
    "tasks.max": "1",
    "genkp.customers.with": "#{Code.isbn10}",
    "genv.customers.name.with": "#{Name.first_name}",
    "genv.customers.visits.with": "#{number.number_between '1','10'}",
    "global.throttle.ms": "500",
    "key.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.StringConverter",
    "value.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.json.JsonConverter",
    "value.converter.schemas.enable": "false"
  }
}

The worker's default converters expect JSON with a schema envelope, so the connector sets its own: plain strings for keys, and JSON without a schema for values. Post the file from the folder that holds it:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:register
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors -d @demo-datagen.json

The reply repeats the configuration, with "tasks":[] and "type":"source". The worker starts the task right after it answers.

docs.title: Read Its Records
docs.text:
The broker creates customers when the connector first writes to it, because automatic topic creation is on by default. This reads the first three records with their keys:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:read
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --topic customers --from-beginning --max-messages 3 --timeout-ms 60000 \
  --formatter-property print.key=true

Each line is a key, a tab and a value such as {"name":"Patrina","visits":"3"}. The names and numbers are random. The consumer ends with Processed a total of 3 messages.

docs.title: Check and Remove It
docs.text:
This reads the connector's status, then deletes it:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:status-remove
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-datagen/status
curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-datagen

The status shows "state":"RUNNING" for the connector and for task 0. A failed task shows FAILED with its error. The worker's log has the rest:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:logs
docker logs --tail 40 connect

After the delete, the last lines of the log say that the worker stopped the task of demo-datagen. Kafka UI at http://127.0.0.1:8086 lists the registered connectors under Kafka Connect, Connectors. Ingest into Iceberg registers a sink connector, the Iceberg sink.

docs.title: PostgreSQL for Debezium
docs.text:
The postgres profile runs PostgreSQL with wal_level=logical. Its init script creates the cdc schema and the cdc_pub publication for every table in that schema, so a Debezium source can read changes to tables you create in cdc. Start both profiles to use it:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/commands.sh:up-postgres
odctl up postgres kafka-lite

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, the REST API is http://connect:8083, and connectors reach the brokers at broker-1:19092, the catalog at http://catalog:8181 and SeaweedFS at http://seaweed:8333.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It holds the configuration above, so it needs no other file:

docs/snippets/kafka-connect/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts kafka-lite, registers a data generator connector, reads three of its
# records, prints the connector's status and removes it.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up kafka-lite

# The REST API answers a little after the worker starts.
until curl -fs http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors >/dev/null; do sleep 2; done

curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors -d @- <<'JSON'
{
  "name": "demo-datagen",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "com.amazonaws.mskdatagen.GeneratorSourceConnector",
    "tasks.max": "1",
    "genkp.customers.with": "#{Code.isbn10}",
    "genv.customers.name.with": "#{Name.first_name}",
    "genv.customers.visits.with": "#{number.number_between '1','10'}",
    "global.throttle.ms": "500",
    "key.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.StringConverter",
    "value.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.json.JsonConverter",
    "value.converter.schemas.enable": "false"
  }
}
JSON
echo

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --topic customers --from-beginning --max-messages 3 --timeout-ms 60000 \
  --formatter-property print.key=true

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-datagen/status
echo
curl -s -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-datagen

It prints the reply to the registration, three records, Processed a total of 3 messages and the status with "state":"RUNNING".

docs.title: Produce and Consume with Kafka
docs.text:
The kafka-lite profile runs one Kafka broker in KRaft mode, the Karapace schema registry, a Kafka Connect worker and Kafka UI. KRaft mode means the brokers keep the cluster's metadata themselves, with no ZooKeeper. kafka-full runs three brokers with the same services beside them. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on Getting Started, which installs odctl and says where the code on this page comes from.

Start the profile:

docs/snippets/kafka/commands.sh:up
odctl up kafka-lite
Endpoint Address Bootstrap servers from the host 127.0.0.1:9092 (kafka-full adds 127.0.0.1:9093 and 127.0.0.1:9094) Bootstrap servers inside the odctl network broker-1:19092 Kafka UI http://127.0.0.1:8086 Schema registry (Karapace) http://127.0.0.1:8081 Kafka Connect REST API http://127.0.0.1:8083

docs.title: Create a Topic
docs.text:
The Kafka command-line tools are in the broker container, which is kafka in kafka-lite and kafka-1 in kafka-full. This creates the topic demo with one partition:

docs/snippets/kafka/commands.sh:create-topic
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --topic demo --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1

The command prints Created topic demo.

docs.title: Produce and Consume
docs.text:
The producer writes five JSON records to demo, and the consumer reads them back from the start of the topic:

docs/snippets/kafka/commands.sh:produce-consume
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo "{\"n\":$i}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic demo

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --topic demo --from-beginning --max-messages 5 --timeout-ms 60000

The consumer prints the five records, {"n":1} to {"n":5}, one per line, and then Processed a total of 5 messages. It reads through a consumer group, so its offsets are stored in the broker's __consumer_offsets topic.

Kafka UI at http://127.0.0.1:8086 shows the topics, their messages, the consumer groups and the schemas in Karapace.

docs.title: Keep Messages Longer
docs.text:
The brokers delete old messages. A partition keeps data for one day or up to 500 MB, and a segment is deleted once either limit is passed. Both limits are set today in .odctl/compose-kafka.yml, where an edit can change them: KAFKA_LOG_RETENTION_MS is 86400000 and KAFKA_LOG_RETENTION_BYTES is 524288000. A topic created without settings takes these values, which this command reads:

docs/snippets/kafka/commands.sh:retention-default
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --describe --all --entity-type topics --entity-name demo | grep -E '^ *retention\.(ms|bytes)='

The output shows retention.ms=86400000 and retention.bytes=524288000. To keep everything in one topic, set retention.ms and retention.bytes to -1 when you create it. -1 means no limit. Other topics keep the broker defaults. This creates the topic history with no limits and describes it:

docs/snippets/kafka/commands.sh:retention-unlimited
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --topic history --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1 \
  --config retention.ms=-1 --config retention.bytes=-1

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --describe --entity-type topics --entity-name history

The describe command lists the settings of that topic: retention.ms=-1 and retention.bytes=-1. retention.bytes applies to each partition, so a topic with three partitions at 500 MB can hold 1.5 GB. To change an existing topic, use kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config with the same two settings. If older messages are missing, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, clients reach the broker at broker-1:19092, and kafka-full adds broker-2:19093 and broker-3:19094. Karapace is http://karapace:8081 and Kafka UI is http://kafka-ui:8080.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It starts kafka-lite, creates demo if it does not exist, writes five records and reads five back:

docs/snippets/kafka/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts kafka-lite, creates the topic demo, writes five records and reads them back.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up kafka-lite

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --if-not-exists --topic demo --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1

for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo "{\"n\":$i}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic demo

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --topic demo --from-beginning --max-messages 5 --timeout-ms 60000

It prints {"n":1} to {"n":5} and Processed a total of 5 messages. When you run it again, it adds five more records and still reads the first five.

docs.title: OpenLineage and Marquez
docs.text:
The lineage profile runs Marquez: an API that receives OpenLineage events and keeps jobs, runs and datasets on PostgreSQL, and a web UI that draws the lineage graph. OpenLineage is an open standard for events that say which job read and wrote which datasets in each run. Anything that sends OpenLineage events over HTTP can report to Marquez. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on Getting Started.

A job sends its events to marquez-api, and marquez-web reads the API to draw the graph:

Start the profile:

docs/snippets/lineage/commands.sh:up
odctl up lineage
Endpoint Address Marquez API from the host http://127.0.0.1:5002 Marquez API inside the odctl network http://marquez-api:5000 Lineage graph UI http://127.0.0.1:3003

docs.title: Send OpenLineage Events
docs.text:
A run is reported as a START event and a COMPLETE event with the same run id. The job reads one dataset and writes another:

docs/snippets/lineage/commands.sh:send
RUN_ID=a1b2c3d4-0000-4000-8000-000000000001
NOW=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.000Z)

for event in START COMPLETE; do
  curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5002/api/v1/lineage \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"eventType\":\"$event\",\"eventTime\":\"$NOW\",
         \"producer\":\"demo\",
         \"run\":{\"runId\":\"$RUN_ID\"},
         \"job\":{\"namespace\":\"demo\",\"name\":\"demo-job\"},
         \"inputs\":[{\"namespace\":\"demo\",\"name\":\"raw-orders\"}],
         \"outputs\":[{\"namespace\":\"demo\",\"name\":\"demo-dataset\"}]}"
done

The run id is a UUID, as OpenLineage requires. Each request prints nothing when Marquez accepts the event.

docs.title: Read the Lineage Back
docs.text:
These read the namespaces, the job and the output dataset back from the API:

docs/snippets/lineage/commands.sh:read
curl http://127.0.0.1:5002/api/v1/namespaces
curl http://127.0.0.1:5002/api/v1/namespaces/demo/jobs/demo-job
curl http://127.0.0.1:5002/api/v1/namespaces/demo/datasets/demo-dataset

Marquez writes the job, the run and the dataset from the events, so all three read back. The first command lists the namespaces, which include demo. The second returns the job demo-job as JSON, with raw-orders among its inputs, demo-dataset among its outputs and a latestRun in state COMPLETED. The third returns the dataset. The UI shows them under the demo namespace.

The UI draws the job between the datasets it read and wrote:

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, send events to http://marquez-api:5000/api/v1/lineage. For an OpenLineage client's HTTP transport, set the URL to http://marquez-api:5000, because the transport adds api/v1/lineage by default.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It gives each run a new id, so it reports a new run every time:

docs/snippets/lineage/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts lineage, reports one run of a job that reads raw-orders and writes
# demo-dataset, and prints the state of the job's latest run.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up lineage

RUN_ID=$(python3 -c 'import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4())')
NOW=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.000Z)
for event in START COMPLETE; do
  curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5002/api/v1/lineage \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"eventType\":\"$event\",\"eventTime\":\"$NOW\",
         \"producer\":\"demo\",
         \"run\":{\"runId\":\"$RUN_ID\"},
         \"job\":{\"namespace\":\"demo\",\"name\":\"demo-job\"},
         \"inputs\":[{\"namespace\":\"demo\",\"name\":\"raw-orders\"}],
         \"outputs\":[{\"namespace\":\"demo\",\"name\":\"demo-dataset\"}]}"
done

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5002/api/v1/namespaces/demo/jobs/demo-job \
  | python3 -c 'import json, sys; run = json.load(sys.stdin)["latestRun"]; print(run["id"], run["state"])'

It prints the new run's id and COMPLETED.

docs.title: MLflow Tracking and Model Serving
docs.text:
The mlflow profile runs two containers. mlflow is the tracking server and model registry, with runs on PostgreSQL and artifacts on SeaweedFS under s3://mlflow. mlflow-serve scores a registered model over HTTP. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on Getting Started. Its last section reads features from Feast with Iceberg.

Your code logs runs and models to the tracking server, and mlflow-serve loads a registered model from it:

Start the profile:

docs/snippets/mlflow/commands.sh:up
odctl up mlflow
Endpoint Address Tracking UI and API from the host http://127.0.0.1:5004 Tracking API inside the odctl network http://mlflow:5000 Model server from the host http://127.0.0.1:5003/invocations Model server inside the odctl network http://mlflow-serve:5003/invocations

The server runs MLflow 3.16.1, so install the same client version on the host.

docs.title: Log a Run with an Artifact
docs.text:
This logs a run with a parameter, a metric and a small file as an artifact, then prints where the artifacts are stored and the run's artifact list:

docs/snippets/mlflow/steps.py:log-run
import pathlib
import mlflow

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://127.0.0.1:5004")
mlflow.set_experiment("demo")

p = pathlib.Path("notes.txt")
p.write_text("hello")
with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    mlflow.log_param("k", "v")
    mlflow.log_metric("m", 1.0)
    mlflow.log_artifact(str(p))

print(mlflow.get_run(run.info.run_id).info.artifact_uri)
print([f.path for f in mlflow.MlflowClient().list_artifacts(run.info.run_id)])

The code prints the artifact URI and the list ['notes.txt']. The artifact URI starts with mlflow-artifacts:/. The server proxies artifacts, so the client uploads through the tracking server and needs no S3 address or keys. Downloads from your machine need one setting, as Load a Model from Your Machine shows. The run and its artifact appear in the UI.

The runs are listed under the experiment in the Model training view:

docs.title: Register a Model
docs.text:
This trains a small XGBoost classifier, registers it as demo-model and points the alias champion at the latest version:

docs/snippets/mlflow/steps.py:register-model
import mlflow, numpy as np, xgboost as xgb
from mlflow import MlflowClient

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://127.0.0.1:5004")
mlflow.set_experiment("demo-model")

X, y = np.array([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0], [3.0]]), np.array([0, 0, 1, 1])
with mlflow.start_run():
    model = xgb.XGBClassifier(n_estimators=5, max_depth=2).fit(X, y)
    mlflow.xgboost.log_model(model, name="model", registered_model_name="demo-model")

client = MlflowClient()
version = max(int(mv.version) for mv in client.search_model_versions("name='demo-model'"))
client.set_registered_model_alias("demo-model", "champion", version)

The run prints Created version '1' of model 'demo-model'. This needs XGBoost on the host. The model server has XGBoost 3.2, so install the same minor version to log a model it can load.

The registry lists each version, with the champion alias on the latest:

docs.title: Serve the Model
docs.text:
mlflow-serve starts with the profile and waits idle while MODEL_URI is empty. MODEL_URI is set in .odctl/.env, which odctl init writes. Change its line there to:

docs/snippets/mlflow/model-uri.env
MODEL_URI="models:/demo-model@champion"

Then replace the containers with odctl recreate mlflow, so mlflow-serve starts with the new value, and score two rows:

docs/snippets/mlflow/commands.sh:serve
odctl recreate mlflow
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5003/invocations \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"inputs": [[0.0], [3.0]]}'

The response is {"predictions": [0, 0]}, one prediction per input row. Check the body rather than the status code, because the server answers 200 with an error payload when scoring fails. http://127.0.0.1:5003/ping answers once the model is loaded.

docs.title: Move the Alias to a New Version
docs.text:
mlflow-serve resolves MODEL_URI once, when its container starts. A new version registered behind an unchanged alias such as champion is not served until you run odctl restart mlflow. Nothing reports an error in the meantime, and the predictions stay those of the old version. To see the change in .env, use a version URI such as models:/demo-model/2 and run odctl recreate mlflow.

Run the code from Register a Model again with min_child_weight=0 added to XGBClassifier. The trees then split, so the new version predicts differently. It registers version 2 and moves champion to it. Then restart the containers and score again:

docs/snippets/mlflow/commands.sh:new-version
odctl restart mlflow
# The server answers nothing while the model loads: 16 seconds in one run.
until curl -fs http://127.0.0.1:5003/ping >/dev/null; do sleep 2; done
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5003/invocations \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"inputs": [[0.0], [3.0]]}'

The predictions now come from version 2: {"predictions": [0, 1]} instead of [0, 0].

docs.title: Load a Model from Your Machine
docs.text:
Uploads go through the tracking server, but a download does not by default. The server then hands the client presigned URLs for http://seaweed:8333, a name that only containers in the odctl network resolve. On your machine, mlflow.artifacts.download_artifacts and a load_model call such as mlflow.sklearn.load_model therefore wait and print no error. Set MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD to false before the call, and the client downloads through the tracking server instead:

docs/snippets/mlflow/steps.py:download
import os

os.environ["MLFLOW_ENABLE_PROXY_MULTIPART_DOWNLOAD"] = "false"
import mlflow

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://127.0.0.1:5004")
path = mlflow.artifacts.download_artifacts("models:/demo-model@champion")
print(sorted(os.listdir(path)))

The output is a listing of the model files that includes MLmodel. mlflow-serve is not affected, because it loads its model inside the odctl network.

docs.title: Serve a Model That Reads Online Features
docs.text:
The MLflow image has no Feast client. A model can still read online features from feast-serve over HTTP, with an mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel whose predict method sends the request. This one reads conv_rate of the driver_pushed feature view from Push Features from Flink SQL and scores a driver 1 when it is above 0.5. Run that section first, so the online store holds conv_rate 0.9 for driver 1001, then save the model class as driver_score.py:

docs/snippets/mlflow/driver_score.py
import mlflow
import requests


class DriverScore(mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel):
    """Scores a driver 1 when the online store holds a conversion rate above 0.5."""

    def predict(self, context, model_input, params=None):
        reply = requests.post(
            "http://feast-serve:6566/get-online-features",
            json={
                "features": ["driver_pushed:conv_rate"],
                "entities": {"driver_id": [int(i) for i in model_input["driver_id"]]},
            },
            timeout=10,
        ).json()
        names = reply["metadata"]["feature_names"]
        rates = reply["results"][names.index("conv_rate")]["values"]
        return [int(rate is not None and rate > 0.5) for rate in rates]


mlflow.models.set_model(DriverScore())

Then register it from a file, so that the server loads the class from the code and not from a copy pickled on your machine. Run this in the folder that holds driver_score.py. It gives the model a signature and no input example, because an example would make MLflow call predict on your machine, where feast-serve does not resolve:

docs/snippets/mlflow/steps.py:features-model
import mlflow, pandas as pd
from mlflow import MlflowClient
from mlflow.models import infer_signature

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://127.0.0.1:5004")
mlflow.set_experiment("driver-score")
with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(
        name="model",
        python_model="driver_score.py",
        pip_requirements=["requests"],
        signature=infer_signature(pd.DataFrame({"driver_id": [1001]}), [1]),
        registered_model_name="driver-score",
    )

client = MlflowClient()
version = max(int(mv.version) for mv in client.search_model_versions("name='driver-score'"))
client.set_registered_model_alias("driver-score", "champion", version)

The run prints three warnings, about integer columns, type hints on predict and the missing input example, and then Created version '1' of model 'driver-score'. The warnings do not stop the registration.

Serve it as in Serve the Model, with this line in .odctl/.env:

docs/snippets/mlflow/model-uri-features.env
MODEL_URI="models:/driver-score@champion"

Run odctl recreate mlflow, then score the driver:

docs/snippets/mlflow/commands.sh:features-score
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5003/invocations \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"dataframe_split": {"columns": ["driver_id"], "data": [[1001]]}}'

The reply is {"predictions": [1]}. Right after apply, feast-serve may not know the feature view yet (see Push Features from Flink SQL), and the reply is an error. Run the command again after a minute. The model costs one HTTP request to feast-serve for each prediction request, and mlflow-serve keeps its 1,500 MB memory limit, which a model with large libraries can reach. The limit is set today by mem_limit in the mlflow-serve service of .odctl/compose-mlops.yml, where an edit can change it.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, set the tracking URI to http://mlflow:5000 and score at http://mlflow-serve:5003/invocations. Airflow tasks use these addresses too. Extra Python packages for both MLflow containers go in _MLOPS_PIP_DEPS in .odctl/.env, followed by odctl recreate mlflow. How It Works says when those packages are installed again.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace, in an environment with mlflow==3.16.1 and XGBoost 3.2 installed. It logs a run, registers demo-model, sets MODEL_URI in .odctl/.env and scores two rows:

docs/snippets/mlflow/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts mlflow, logs a run with an artifact, registers an XGBoost model with
# the alias champion, serves it with mlflow-serve and scores two rows. Run it
# in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace, in an environment with
# mlflow==3.16.1 and xgboost 3.2 installed.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up mlflow

python - <<'PY'
import pathlib
import mlflow, numpy as np, xgboost as xgb
from mlflow import MlflowClient

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://127.0.0.1:5004")

mlflow.set_experiment("demo")
p = pathlib.Path("notes.txt")
p.write_text("hello")
with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    mlflow.log_param("k", "v")
    mlflow.log_metric("m", 1.0)
    mlflow.log_artifact(str(p))
print(mlflow.get_run(run.info.run_id).info.artifact_uri)

mlflow.set_experiment("demo-model")
X, y = np.array([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0], [3.0]]), np.array([0, 0, 1, 1])
with mlflow.start_run():
    model = xgb.XGBClassifier(n_estimators=5, max_depth=2).fit(X, y)
    mlflow.xgboost.log_model(model, name="model", registered_model_name="demo-model")
client = MlflowClient()
version = max(int(mv.version) for mv in client.search_model_versions("name='demo-model'"))
client.set_registered_model_alias("demo-model", "champion", version)
PY

# Serve the champion: set MODEL_URI in the workspace and replace the containers.
sed -i.bak 's|^MODEL_URI=.*|MODEL_URI="models:/demo-model@champion"|' .odctl/.env
odctl recreate mlflow
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5003/invocations \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"inputs": [[0.0], [3.0]]}'
echo

It prints the artifact URI, Created version with the new version number, the recreate messages and {"predictions": [0, 0]}. The sed command keeps the old .env as .odctl/.env.bak.

docs.title: Catalogue a Database with OpenMetadata
docs.text:
A data catalogue lists the databases, tables and columns of an organisation, so people can search them and see who owns each one. The metadata profile runs OpenMetadata, a data catalogue: the server with its UI and REST API, Elasticsearch for search, and an ingestion container. The ingestion container is an Airflow that runs the ingestion pipelines the server deploys. Its own tables are in the omt database on PostgreSQL. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on Getting Started. It uses the PostgreSQL that the profile starts as the database to catalogue.

Start the profile:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:up
odctl up metadata
Endpoint Address UI and REST API from the host http://127.0.0.1:8585 UI and REST API inside the odctl network http://openmetadata-server:8585 Ingestion Airflow from the host http://127.0.0.1:8087

Log in as admin@open-data.local with the password admin. The domain is open-data.local, not the upstream default, and a wrong domain fails with an invalid password error.

docs.title: Get a Token
docs.text:
The login API takes the password base64-encoded and returns a JWT, a signed token that later requests send in the Authorization header. This sets TOKEN and AUTH for the next steps, and prints nothing:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:login
TOKEN=$(curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"email\":\"admin@open-data.local\",\"password\":\"$(printf admin | base64)\"}" \
  http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/users/login \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["accessToken"])')
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

docs.title: Register PostgreSQL as a Database Service
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is already running, so it serves as the source. The server reaches it by its container name. This sets SVC to the id of the new service:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:service
SVC=$(curl -s -X PUT -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"demo_pg","serviceType":"Postgres","connection":{"config":{"type":"Postgres","scheme":"postgresql+psycopg2","username":"user","authType":{"password":"password"},"hostPort":"postgres:5432","database":"omt"}}}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/databaseServices \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["id"])')

docs.title: Run a Metadata Ingestion
docs.text:
Create a pipeline, deploy it as a DAG into the ingestion Airflow, and trigger it:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:pipeline
PIPE=$(curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"name\":\"demo_pg_metadata\",\"pipelineType\":\"metadata\",\"service\":{\"id\":\"$SVC\",\"type\":\"databaseService\"},\"sourceConfig\":{\"config\":{\"type\":\"DatabaseMetadata\"}},\"airflowConfig\":{\"startDate\":\"2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z\"}}" \
  http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/ingestionPipelines \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["id"])')

curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/ingestionPipelines/deploy/$PIPE
curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/ingestionPipelines/trigger/$PIPE

The deploy answers that the pipeline has been created. It works once the ingestion Airflow answers at http://127.0.0.1:8087/api/v2/monitor/health, which can be some time after odctl up metadata returns. Airflow has to parse the new DAG file before the trigger works, so repeat the trigger every few seconds until it answers that the pipeline has been triggered. Then read the run's state:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:status
curl -s -H "$AUTH" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/ingestionPipelines/name/demo_pg.demo_pg_metadata?fields=pipelineStatuses"

The reply is the pipeline as JSON. The pipelineState of the first entry of pipelineStatuses reaches success when the tables are catalogued. They then appear in the UI under the demo_pg service.

docs.title: Search the Catalogue
docs.text:
Rebuild the search index, then query it:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:search
curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/apps/trigger/SearchIndexingApplication
curl -s -H "$AUTH" "http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/search/query?q=*&index=table_search_index&size=1"

The search reply is JSON, and hits.total.value counts the searchable tables. The index fills over a few minutes after the rebuild, and then holds more than 100 tables: OpenMetadata's own tables in the omt database.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, call the API at http://openmetadata-server:8585. The server also answers the Model Context Protocol at http://127.0.0.1:8585/mcp with the same token.

docs.title: Remove the Example
docs.text:
This deletes the service with its pipeline and the tables it catalogued:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/commands.sh:remove
curl -s -X DELETE -H "$AUTH" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1/services/databaseServices/name/demo_pg?hardDelete=true&recursive=true"

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It runs every step above, waits where a step needs time, and removes the service at the end:

docs/snippets/openmetadata/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts metadata, registers PostgreSQL as a database service, runs a metadata
# ingestion of the omt database, counts the searchable tables and removes the
# service again.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up metadata
om=http://127.0.0.1:8585/api/v1
json() { python3 -c "import json, sys; print($1)"; }

TOKEN=$(curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"email\":\"admin@open-data.local\",\"password\":\"$(printf admin | base64)\"}" \
  "$om/users/login" | json 'json.load(sys.stdin)["accessToken"]')
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

SVC=$(curl -s -X PUT -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"demo_pg","serviceType":"Postgres","connection":{"config":{"type":"Postgres","scheme":"postgresql+psycopg2","username":"user","authType":{"password":"password"},"hostPort":"postgres:5432","database":"omt"}}}' \
  "$om/services/databaseServices" | json 'json.load(sys.stdin)["id"]')

PIPE=$(curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"name\":\"demo_pg_metadata\",\"pipelineType\":\"metadata\",\"service\":{\"id\":\"$SVC\",\"type\":\"databaseService\"},\"sourceConfig\":{\"config\":{\"type\":\"DatabaseMetadata\"}},\"airflowConfig\":{\"startDate\":\"2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z\"}}" \
  "$om/services/ingestionPipelines" | json 'json.load(sys.stdin)["id"]')
# The server deploys the pipeline into the ingestion Airflow, which answers a
# little after the server.
until curl -fs http://127.0.0.1:8087/api/v2/monitor/health >/dev/null; do sleep 5; done
until curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" "$om/services/ingestionPipelines/deploy/$PIPE" \
  | grep 'has been created' >/dev/null; do sleep 5; done

# Airflow parses the new DAG file before the trigger works.
until curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" "$om/services/ingestionPipelines/trigger/$PIPE" \
  | grep 'has been triggered' >/dev/null; do sleep 5; done

state=""
until [ "$state" = success ] || [ "$state" = failed ]; do
  sleep 10
  state=$(curl -s -H "$AUTH" \
    "$om/services/ingestionPipelines/name/demo_pg.demo_pg_metadata?fields=pipelineStatuses" \
    | json '(json.load(sys.stdin).get("pipelineStatuses") or [{}])[0].get("pipelineState", "")')
done
echo "ingestion: $state"

# The search index fills over a few minutes after it is rebuilt.
curl -s -X POST -H "$AUTH" "$om/apps/trigger/SearchIndexingApplication" >/dev/null
hits=0
until [ "$hits" -gt 100 ]; do
  sleep 5
  hits=$(curl -s -H "$AUTH" "$om/search/query?q=*&index=table_search_index&size=1" \
    | json 'json.load(sys.stdin)["hits"]["total"]["value"]')
done
echo "searchable tables: $hits"

curl -s -X DELETE -H "$AUTH" \
  "$om/services/databaseServices/name/demo_pg?hardDelete=true&recursive=true" >/dev/null
echo "removed demo_pg"

It prints ingestion: success, the number of searchable tables, which is more than 100, and removed demo_pg. The whole run takes several minutes.

docs.title: Rolling Windows in Flink SQL
docs.text:
A feature such as the sum of a card's payments over the last 10 minutes, 1 hour and 1 day needs one rolling window for each size. A rolling window, or OVER window in SQL, aggregates the rows of a key that fall within a time range before each new row. Flink SQL refuses two different OVER windows in one streaming query, so this guide shows the two ways around it. The end-to-end tests run the SQL below on every release.

This guide builds on Flink SQL, which opens the SQL client and writes to PostgreSQL over JDBC. It needs only flink-lite, which starts PostgreSQL through the catalog:

docs/snippets/rolling-windows/commands.sh:up
odctl up flink-lite

The endpoints are those of Flink SQL. Open the SQL client:

docs/snippets/rolling-windows/commands.sh:sql-client
docker exec -it flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh

docs.title: One Query Cannot Hold Two Windows
docs.text:
Flink's documentation says that for streaming queries the OVER windows of all aggregates in one SELECT must be identical (Over aggregation, Flink 2.2). These statements declare 20 generated payments, one a minute for two cards, and ask for a 10-minute and a 1-hour sum in one query:

docs/snippets/rolling-windows/steps.sql:windows-refused
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'streaming';
CREATE TABLE payments (card BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, seq BIGINT, ts AS TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(seq * 60000, 3), WATERMARK FOR ts AS ts) WITH ('connector'='datagen','fields.seq.kind'='sequence','fields.seq.start'='1','fields.seq.end'='20','fields.card.min'='1','fields.card.max'='2','fields.amount.min'='1','fields.amount.max'='10');
SELECT card,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '10' MINUTE PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS sum_10m,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' HOUR PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS sum_1h
FROM payments;

The client prints [ERROR] Could not execute SQL statement. with this reason:

org.apache.flink.table.api.TableException: Over Agg: Unsupported use of OVER windows. All aggregates must be computed on the same window. please re-check the over window statement.

docs.title: One Statement for Each Window Size
docs.text:
The first route is one statement for each window size, each writing its own table. This creates the two PostgreSQL tables:

docs/snippets/rolling-windows/commands.sh:create-window-tables
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  CREATE TABLE card_sum_10m (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE PRECISION);
  CREATE TABLE card_sum_1h (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE PRECISION);"

Then run the two statements in a new SQL client session. The sequence field makes the source stop after 20 rows, and the event time ts makes each job write every row before it finishes. An OVER window on PROCTIME() would lose the rows still waiting for their timer when a bounded source ends:

docs/snippets/rolling-windows/steps.sql:windows-one-per-size
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'streaming';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE payments (card BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, seq BIGINT, ts AS TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(seq * 60000, 3), WATERMARK FOR ts AS ts) WITH ('connector'='datagen','fields.seq.kind'='sequence','fields.seq.start'='1','fields.seq.end'='20','fields.card.min'='1','fields.card.max'='2','fields.amount.min'='1','fields.amount.max'='10');
CREATE TABLE sum_10m (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='card_sum_10m','username'='user','password'='password');
CREATE TABLE sum_1h (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='card_sum_1h','username'='user','password'='password');
INSERT INTO sum_10m SELECT card, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '10' MINUTE PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM payments;
INSERT INTO sum_1h SELECT card, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' HOUR PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM payments;

Each INSERT prints [INFO] Complete execution of the SQL update statement. once its job ends. This counts the rows of both tables:

docs/snippets/rolling-windows/commands.sh:check-windows
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM card_sum_10m) AS rows_10m, (SELECT count(*) FROM card_sum_1h) AS rows_1h"

Each table holds 20 rows, one for each payment:

 rows_10m | rows_1h
----------+---------
       20 |      20
(1 row)

The cost is one job for each window size, each reading the source again, and one table for each size that a reader has to join on the key. With four sizes that is four jobs.

docs.title: One Function for Every Size
docs.text:
The second route is one KeyedProcessFunction in the DataStream API, which keeps the events of the longest window in Flink state and computes every size from them. This sketch is not run by the end-to-end tests:

docs/snippets/rolling-windows/keyed_sketch.py:keyed-sketch
from pyflink.common import Types
from pyflink.datastream.functions import KeyedProcessFunction, RuntimeContext
from pyflink.datastream.state import ListStateDescriptor

WINDOWS_MS = {"10m": 600_000, "1h": 3_600_000, "1d": 86_400_000, "7d": 604_800_000}


class RollingSums(KeyedProcessFunction):
    def open(self, runtime_context: RuntimeContext):
        # Every event of the longest window, for each key, kept in Flink state.
        self.events = runtime_context.get_list_state(
            ListStateDescriptor("events", Types.TUPLE([Types.LONG(), Types.DOUBLE()]))
        )

    def process_element(self, value, ctx):
        now = ctx.timestamp()
        kept = [(t, a) for t, a in self.events.get() if now - t <= WINDOWS_MS["7d"]]
        kept.append((now, value[1]))
        self.events.update(kept)
        yield value[0], {n: sum(a for t, a in kept if now - t <= ms) for n, ms in WINDOWS_MS.items()}

One job computes all sizes, but you write and test the code in Python or Java instead of SQL, and you manage the state, which grows with the events of the longest window for each key.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, the addresses are those of Flink SQL: Flink's REST API is http://jobmanager:8081 and PostgreSQL is jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It runs the first route with tables of its own for each run, so it can run again:

docs/snippets/rolling-windows/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts flink-lite, computes a 10-minute and a 1-hour rolling sum over 20
# generated payments, one Flink SQL statement for each window size, and prints
# how many rows each wrote to PostgreSQL. Each run uses its own table names.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up flink-lite

run=$(date +%s)
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  CREATE TABLE card_sum_10m_$run (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE PRECISION);
  CREATE TABLE card_sum_1h_$run (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE PRECISION);"

docker exec -i flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh <<SQL | grep -E 'ERROR|Exception' || true
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'streaming';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE payments (card BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, seq BIGINT, ts AS TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(seq * 60000, 3), WATERMARK FOR ts AS ts) WITH ('connector'='datagen','fields.seq.kind'='sequence','fields.seq.start'='1','fields.seq.end'='20','fields.card.min'='1','fields.card.max'='2','fields.amount.min'='1','fields.amount.max'='10');
CREATE TABLE sum_10m (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='card_sum_10m_$run','username'='user','password'='password');
CREATE TABLE sum_1h (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='card_sum_1h_$run','username'='user','password'='password');
INSERT INTO sum_10m SELECT card, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '10' MINUTE PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM payments;
INSERT INTO sum_1h SELECT card, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' HOUR PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM payments;
SQL

docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM card_sum_10m_$run) AS rows_10m, (SELECT count(*) FROM card_sum_1h_$run) AS rows_1h"

It prints rows_10m and rows_1h as 20 and 20.

docs.title: Spark
docs.text:
The spark-lite profile runs a Spark master, one worker and the Spark History Server. spark-full runs three workers. Spark's default catalog is iceberg, already pointed at the Iceberg REST catalog, so spark-sql reads and writes Iceberg tables with no extra settings. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on Kafka, which writes and reads a topic, and Flink SQL, whose Avro records the last step reads. Start the profile:

docs/snippets/spark/commands.sh:up
odctl up spark-lite
Endpoint Address Spark master UI from the host http://127.0.0.1:9080 Master URL from the host spark://127.0.0.1:7077 Spark History Server from the host http://127.0.0.1:18080 Master URL inside the odctl network spark://spark-master:7077 Spark History Server inside the odctl network http://spark-history:18080

docs.title: Run SQL Against Iceberg
docs.text:
This creates a namespace and a table in the iceberg catalog, inserts three rows and counts them:

docs/snippets/spark/commands.sh:run-sql
docker exec spark-master /opt/spark/bin/spark-sql -e "
  CREATE NAMESPACE IF NOT EXISTS iceberg.demo;
  CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE iceberg.demo.t (id BIGINT) USING iceberg;
  INSERT INTO iceberg.demo.t VALUES (1),(2),(3);
  SELECT count(*) FROM iceberg.demo.t;"

The query prints 3. The table is in the same catalog that Flink, Kafka Connect and Trino use, and Ingest into Iceberg shows the other engines writing to it.

docs.title: See Finished Applications
docs.text:
Every Spark application writes an event log to /tmp/spark-events, which all Spark containers share. This lists the logs:

docs/snippets/spark/commands.sh:event-logs
docker exec spark-master ls /tmp/spark-events

The command prints one name per application, such as eventlog_v2_local-1792817297659. The Spark History Server at http://127.0.0.1:18080 reads the same directory, so the spark-sql run above appears there after it ends, with its jobs, stages and SQL plans. The master UI at http://127.0.0.1:9080 shows the workers and the applications the master has run.

The event logs are on a volume held in memory, so odctl down removes them.

The History Server lists the spark-sql run:

The master UI at http://127.0.0.1:9080 lists the worker:

docs.title: Read a Kafka Topic
docs.text:
The Kafka connector for Spark is in the shared volume with its dependencies, so a job reads Kafka with no --packages option. Start kafka-lite beside Spark:

docs/snippets/spark/commands.sh:up-kafka-lite
odctl up kafka-lite

This creates the topic spark-demo and writes three messages to it:

docs/snippets/spark/commands.sh:kafka-topic
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --topic spark-demo --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1

for i in 1 2 3; do echo "{\"n\":$i}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic spark-demo

Save this PySpark job as read_kafka.py. A batch read with spark.read reads the topic from its first offset to its last and then ends:

docs/snippets/spark/read_kafka.py
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("read-kafka").getOrCreate()

df = (
    spark.read.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker-1:19092")
    .option("subscribe", "spark-demo")
    .load()
)
df.selectExpr("CAST(value AS STRING) AS value").orderBy("value").show(truncate=False)

Copy the file into the master container and submit it:

docs/snippets/spark/commands.sh:kafka-read
docker cp read_kafka.py spark-master:/tmp/read_kafka.py
docker exec spark-master /opt/spark/bin/spark-submit /tmp/read_kafka.py

The job prints a table with the values {"n":1}, {"n":2} and {"n":3}. Kafka returns each message as binary key and value columns, with the topic, partition, offset, timestamp and timestampType beside them.

docs.title: Read Avro Records Written with the Schema Registry
docs.text:
The orders topic that Flink SQL fills holds Avro records written with the Karapace schema registry. Each value is a zero byte, the 4-byte id of the schema, and then the record in Avro's binary encoding, so Spark cannot read it as text. Save this job as read_avro.py. It gets the latest schema of the subject orders-value from Karapace, drops the 5 bytes and decodes the rest with from_avro, which needs no --packages option because the Avro module is in the shared volume. This works when all records were written with the subject's latest schema version. If the Flink section has not run, the job stops with HTTP Error 404: Not Found, because the subject does not exist yet.

docs/snippets/spark/read_avro.py
import json
import urllib.request

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.avro.functions import from_avro
from pyspark.sql.functions import expr

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("read-avro").getOrCreate()

# The latest schema of the subject, as the schema registry holds it.
url = "http://karapace:8081/subjects/orders-value/versions/latest"
with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=30) as reply:
    schema = json.load(reply)["schema"]

raw = (
    spark.read.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker-1:19092")
    .option("subscribe", "orders")
    .load()
)

# Skip the first 5 bytes of each value: a zero byte and the 4-byte schema id.
orders = raw.select(
    from_avro(expr("substring(value, 6, length(value) - 5)"), schema).alias("order")
).select("order.*")
orders.orderBy("supplier", "price").show()

Copy the file into the master container and submit it:

docs/snippets/spark/commands.sh:avro-read
docker cp read_avro.py spark-master:/tmp/read_avro.py
docker exec spark-master /opt/spark/bin/spark-submit /tmp/read_avro.py

The job prints a table with the columns supplier and price, and the rows a 5.0, a 10.0 and b 7.5.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, submit applications to spark://spark-master:7077. Spark's settings, including the catalog and S3 access to SeaweedFS, are in spark/spark-defaults.conf in the workspace.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It runs the Iceberg and Kafka steps above with a table and a topic of its own for each run, and writes the PySpark job into the master container itself:

docs/snippets/spark/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts spark-lite and kafka-lite, writes and counts an Iceberg table with
# spark-sql, then writes three messages to a topic and reads them with a
# PySpark batch job. Each run uses its own table and topic names.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up spark-lite kafka-lite

run=$(date +%s)
docker exec spark-master /opt/spark/bin/spark-sql -e "
  CREATE NAMESPACE IF NOT EXISTS iceberg.demo;
  CREATE TABLE iceberg.demo.t_$run (id BIGINT) USING iceberg;
  INSERT INTO iceberg.demo.t_$run VALUES (1),(2),(3);
  SELECT count(*) FROM iceberg.demo.t_$run;" 2>/dev/null

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --topic "spark-$run" --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
for i in 1 2 3; do echo "{\"n\":$i}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic "spark-$run"

docker exec -i spark-master sh -c "cat > /tmp/read_kafka_$run.py" <<PY
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("read-kafka").getOrCreate()
df = (
    spark.read.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker-1:19092")
    .option("subscribe", "spark-$run")
    .load()
)
df.selectExpr("CAST(value AS STRING) AS value").orderBy("value").show(truncate=False)
PY
docker exec spark-master /opt/spark/bin/spark-submit "/tmp/read_kafka_$run.py" 2>/dev/null

It prints 3, Created topic with the topic's name, and a table with the values {"n":1}, {"n":2} and {"n":3}.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
The telemetry profile runs the grafana/otel-lgtm image: an OpenTelemetry Collector, Prometheus, Tempo, Loki and Grafana in one container. OpenTelemetry is an open standard for metrics, traces and logs, and OTLP is its protocol for sending them. Tempo stores traces, Loki stores logs, and Grafana draws dashboards from all three stores.

This guide builds on Getting Started. Start the profile next to the profiles you want to watch:

docs/snippets/telemetry/commands.sh:up
odctl up telemetry kafka-lite flink-lite

Prometheus reads metrics from the services, and the collector receives OTLP and passes each kind of data to its store:

Endpoint Address Grafana (user user, password password) http://127.0.0.1:3004 Prometheus http://127.0.0.1:19090 OTLP through the collector 127.0.0.1:4317 (gRPC), http://127.0.0.1:4318 (HTTP)

docs.title: Where the Metrics Come From
docs.text: Prometheus scrapes the services that publish a metrics endpoint, by container name on the odctl network. Airflow pushes its metrics over OTLP to the collector, and the collector reads PostgreSQL and Valkey directly. A service that is not running is a target that is down.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text:
Grafana has a dashboard per service in a folder named odctl. A dashboard fills in once its service's profile is up. The dashboards are JSON files in .odctl/grafana/dashboards/. Edit a file and run odctl restart telemetry to load it. Changes made in the Grafana UI are not kept.

For example, the PostgreSQL dashboard:

docs.title: Send Your Own Metrics
docs.text:
Point an OpenTelemetry SDK at http://127.0.0.1:4318, its default HTTP port. The end-to-end tests post one metric with curl, which shows the path:

docs/snippets/telemetry/commands.sh:send-metric
ts=$(python3 -c "import time;print(int(time.time()*1e9))")
cat > /tmp/otlp.json <<JSON
{"resourceMetrics":[{"resource":{"attributes":[{"key":"service.name","value":{"stringValue":"demo"}}]},
"scopeMetrics":[{"scope":{"name":"demo"},"metrics":[{"name":"demo_total","unit":"1",
"sum":{"aggregationTemporality":2,"isMonotonic":true,"dataPoints":[
{"asDouble":42,"timeUnixNano":"${ts}","startTimeUnixNano":"${ts}","attributes":[]}]}}]}]}]}
JSON
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data-binary @/tmp/otlp.json \
  http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/metrics
curl "http://127.0.0.1:19090/api/v1/query?query=demo_total"

The collector answers {"partialSuccess":{}}. The collector passes metrics on in batches, so the query can come back empty for a few seconds. Then its result holds demo_total with the value "42". Prometheus also accepts OTLP metrics directly at http://127.0.0.1:19090/api/v1/otlp/v1/metrics.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, send OTLP to the collector at otel-lgtm:4317 (gRPC) or http://otel-lgtm:4318 (HTTP), as Airflow does. Prometheus is http://otel-lgtm:9090 and Grafana is http://otel-lgtm:3000.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It waits until Prometheus returns the metric:

docs/snippets/telemetry/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts telemetry, sends one OTLP metric to the collector and waits until
# Prometheus returns it.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up telemetry

ts=$(python3 -c "import time;print(int(time.time()*1e9))")
curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/metrics -d @- <<JSON
{"resourceMetrics":[{"resource":{"attributes":[{"key":"service.name","value":{"stringValue":"demo"}}]},
"scopeMetrics":[{"scope":{"name":"demo"},"metrics":[{"name":"demo_total","unit":"1",
"sum":{"aggregationTemporality":2,"isMonotonic":true,"dataPoints":[
{"asDouble":42,"timeUnixNano":"${ts}","startTimeUnixNano":"${ts}","attributes":[]}]}}]}]}]}
JSON
echo

# The collector passes metrics on in batches, so the first queries can be empty.
until curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:19090/api/v1/query?query=demo_total" | grep '"42"' >/dev/null; do
  sleep 2
done
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:19090/api/v1/query?query=demo_total"
echo

It prints the collector's answer and then the query result, with demo_total and the value "42".

docs.title: Temporal Workers
docs.text:
Temporal runs long-running code that survives failures: a workflow is a function whose progress the server records, and an activity is a step of it that can fail and be retried. The temporal profile runs the Temporal development server: the server, the Web UI and a SQLite database in one container. odctl runs only the server. Your own process runs the worker that executes workflows and activities. The end-to-end tests run the code below on every release.

This guide builds on Getting Started. Start the profile and install the Python SDK at the version the tests use:

docs/snippets/temporal-workers/commands.sh:install
odctl up temporal
pip install temporalio==1.34.0
Endpoint Address gRPC from the host, namespace default 127.0.0.1:7233 gRPC inside the odctl network temporal:7233 Web UI http://127.0.0.1:8233

docs.title: A Worker and a Workflow
docs.text:
Save this code as greet.py and run it with python greet.py. It starts a worker, runs the workflow Greet on it and prints the result. The activity fails on its first attempt, so the result shows that the retry policy ran it again:

docs/snippets/temporal-workers/steps.py:worker
import asyncio
from datetime import timedelta
from temporalio import activity, workflow
from temporalio.client import Client
from temporalio.common import RetryPolicy
from temporalio.worker import Worker


@activity.defn
async def greet(name: str) -> str:
    if activity.info().attempt < 2:
        raise RuntimeError("first attempt fails on purpose")
    return f"hello {name}"


@workflow.defn
class Greet:
    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, name: str) -> str:
        return await workflow.execute_activity(
            greet, name,
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(seconds=30),
            retry_policy=RetryPolicy(initial_interval=timedelta(seconds=1), maximum_attempts=3),
        )


async def main() -> None:
    client = await Client.connect("127.0.0.1:7233")
    async with Worker(client, task_queue="demo", workflows=[Greet], activities=[greet]):
        print(await client.execute_workflow(Greet.run, "odctl", id="greet-1", task_queue="demo"))


# The workflow sandbox imports this file again, so run main only as a script.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

The worker logs the RuntimeError of the first attempt with its traceback, and then the script prints hello odctl.

docs.title: Wait for an Approval
docs.text:
A workflow can wait for a signal, for example a person approving an agent's action. The workflow below waits until its approve signal arrives, and then returns who approved it:

docs/snippets/temporal-workers/steps.py:approval-workflow
@workflow.defn
class Approval:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.approver = None

    @workflow.signal
    def approve(self, approver: str) -> None:
        self.approver = approver

    @workflow.run
    async def run(self) -> str:
        await workflow.wait_condition(lambda: self.approver is not None)
        return f"approved by {self.approver}"

Add the class to greet.py and replace main with this one, which registers both workflows with the worker, runs Greet, starts Approval and sends its signal:

docs/snippets/temporal-workers/steps.py:approval-run
async def main() -> None:
    client = await Client.connect("127.0.0.1:7233")
    async with Worker(client, task_queue="demo", workflows=[Greet, Approval], activities=[greet]):
        print(await client.execute_workflow(Greet.run, "odctl", id="greet-1", task_queue="demo"))
        handle = await client.start_workflow(Approval.run, id="approval-1", task_queue="demo")
        await handle.signal(Approval.approve, "alice")
        print(await handle.result())

The script prints hello odctl and then approved by alice. The complete file is the runnable example below. Until the signal arrives, the Web UI lists the workflow as running.

The Web UI at http://127.0.0.1:8233 lists each workflow. Here approval-2 was started without a signal, so it is still running:

docs.title: History
docs.text: Workflow history is in the database file inside the container. It survives odctl restart temporal, and the tests check that a workflow left waiting for its signal resumes and completes afterwards. odctl down removes the history.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, a worker connects to temporal:7233 with the namespace default.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.py and run it with python example.py while the temporal profile is up, in an environment with temporalio==1.34.0. It is greet.py with both steps above:

docs/snippets/temporal-workers/example.py
"""A Temporal worker with two workflows: one retries a failing activity, the other
waits for an approval signal. Run it with odctl's temporal profile up."""

import asyncio
from datetime import timedelta
from temporalio import activity, workflow
from temporalio.client import Client
from temporalio.common import RetryPolicy
from temporalio.worker import Worker


@activity.defn
async def greet(name: str) -> str:
    if activity.info().attempt < 2:
        raise RuntimeError("first attempt fails on purpose")
    return f"hello {name}"


@workflow.defn
class Greet:
    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, name: str) -> str:
        return await workflow.execute_activity(
            greet, name,
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(seconds=30),
            retry_policy=RetryPolicy(initial_interval=timedelta(seconds=1), maximum_attempts=3),
        )


@workflow.defn
class Approval:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.approver = None

    @workflow.signal
    def approve(self, approver: str) -> None:
        self.approver = approver

    @workflow.run
    async def run(self) -> str:
        await workflow.wait_condition(lambda: self.approver is not None)
        return f"approved by {self.approver}"


async def main() -> None:
    client = await Client.connect("127.0.0.1:7233")
    async with Worker(client, task_queue="demo", workflows=[Greet, Approval], activities=[greet]):
        print(await client.execute_workflow(Greet.run, "odctl", id="greet-1", task_queue="demo"))
        handle = await client.start_workflow(Approval.run, id="approval-1", task_queue="demo")
        await handle.signal(Approval.approve, "alice")
        print(await handle.result())


# The workflow sandbox imports this file again, so run main only as a script.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

It prints hello odctl and then approved by alice. It can run again, because Temporal accepts a new run of a workflow id whose last run has completed.

docs.title: Trino and Metabase
docs.text:
The trino profile runs Trino, which queries PostgreSQL, Iceberg, ClickHouse, Kafka and Valkey through one SQL interface. The metabase profile runs Metabase, which draws charts and dashboards over those databases. Metabase keeps its own settings and dashboards in PostgreSQL, so both profiles start postgres. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on Getting Started. The catalogs read the services of earlier guides, such as Kafka, Ingest into Iceberg and ClickHouse, when their profiles are running. Start both profiles:

docs/snippets/trino-metabase/commands.sh:up
odctl up trino metabase
Endpoint Address Trino UI and JDBC from the host http://127.0.0.1:8080 Metabase from the host http://127.0.0.1:3000

docs.title: Trino Catalogs
docs.text:
A Trino catalog is a configured connection to one data source. This lists them:

docs/snippets/trino-metabase/commands.sh:catalogs
docker exec trino trino --execute "SHOW CATALOGS"

The command prints "clickhouse", "iceberg", "kafka", "postgres", "system" and "valkey", one per line, with a Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS line before them:

Catalog Reads Needs postgres the odctl database nothing more iceberg tables in the REST catalog, with files on SeaweedFS catalog clickhouse the feature_store database on ch-11 ch-lite or ch-full kafka topics, with fields from the Karapace schema registry kafka-lite or kafka-full valkey keys in Valkey valkey

Every catalog loads when Trino starts, even when its service is not running. A query against such a catalog fails until you start that profile. Catalogs finish loading after Trino's health endpoint starts answering, so SHOW CATALOGS can take a minute to list them all.

This runs a query with no table:

docs/snippets/trino-metabase/commands.sh:query
docker exec trino trino --execute "SELECT 1"

It prints "1". Trino has no password authentication, so it accepts any user name. docker exec -it trino trino connects as trino. Pass --user user to use the name the rest of the stack uses. Trino Access Rules explains the rules in trino/rules.json.

The Trino UI at http://127.0.0.1:8080 asks only for a user name. It shows the cluster and the queries that ran in the last few minutes.

docs.title: Metabase
docs.text:
Open http://127.0.0.1:3000 and create the first admin account. Then add each database under Admin settings, Databases, with these settings:

Database type Host Port Other settings PostgreSQL postgres 5432 database odctl, user user, password password ClickHouse ch-11 8123 database default, user default, password password, no SSL Starburst (for Trino) trino 8080 catalog postgres, schema public, user admin, no SSL

Metabase runs inside the odctl network, so it reaches each database by container name. Use the Starburst driver for Trino, because it is the Trino driver Metabase ships. It needs a catalog, and any catalog in the table above works.

Metabase takes a while to start. It is ready when this request answers {"status":"ok"}:

docs/snippets/trino-metabase/commands.sh:metabase-health
curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/health

A SQL question on the PostgreSQL connection, shown as a bar chart:

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, Trino is at http://trino:8080 and Metabase at http://metabase:3000.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It waits for the catalogs and for Metabase before it runs the commands above:

docs/snippets/trino-metabase/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts trino and metabase, waits until every Trino catalog has loaded and
# Metabase answers, then lists the catalogs and runs a query.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up trino metabase

# Catalogs finish loading after Trino's health endpoint answers.
until docker exec trino trino --execute "SHOW CATALOGS" 2>/dev/null | grep '"valkey"' >/dev/null; do sleep 5; done
docker exec trino trino --execute "SHOW CATALOGS"
docker exec trino trino --execute "SELECT 1"

until curl -fs http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/health; do sleep 5; done
echo

It prints the six catalogs, "1" and {"status":"ok"}.

docs.title: Valkey
docs.text:
The valkey profile runs the Valkey Bundle image as one container named valkey. Valkey is an in-memory key-value store that speaks the Redis protocol. The Bundle image adds modules for JSON documents, Bloom filters and vector search. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on Getting Started.

Start the profile:

docs/snippets/valkey/commands.sh:up
odctl up valkey
Setting Value Address from the host 127.0.0.1:6379 Address inside the odctl network valkey:6379 User user, password password Memory limit 512 MB

The memory limit is set today by mem_limit in the valkey service of .odctl/compose-store.yml, where an edit can change it.

docs.title: Users and Permissions
docs.text: The unauthenticated default user is turned off, so every client logs in as user. That user has every command, every key pattern and every Pub/Sub channel. Channels are a separate permission in Valkey, and the profile grants them explicitly, so PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE work as well as key commands.

docs.title: Write and Read Keys
docs.text:
valkey-cli is in the container. Log in with a URL that carries the user and password:

docs/snippets/valkey/commands.sh:round-trip
vk=redis://user:password@localhost:6379
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" ping
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" mset 'model:1' '{"a":1}' 'model:2' '{"a":2}'
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" mget 'model:1' 'model:2'
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" del 'model:1' 'model:2'

--no-auth-warning stops valkey-cli printing a warning about the password on the command line. ping answers PONG. mset writes both keys in one command and prints OK. mget reads them back in one round trip and prints {"a":1} and {"a":2}. del prints 2, the number of keys it removed.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: Valkey writes an append-only file and saves a snapshot every 60 seconds when at least one key has changed. Both settings are in the command of the valkey service in .odctl/compose-store.yml (--appendonly yes and --save 60 1). Both files are inside the container, so a restart keeps the data and odctl down removes it.

docs.title: From Another Container
docs.text: Inside the odctl network, connect to valkey:6379 with the same user and password, for example redis://user:password@valkey:6379 for a Redis client. Feast's online store uses this address, as Feast with Iceberg shows.

docs.title: Runnable Example
docs.text:
Save this file as example.sh and run it with bash example.sh in the folder that holds your .odctl workspace. It also stores a JSON document with the JSON module and reads one field of it:

docs/snippets/valkey/example.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts valkey, writes two keys and reads them back, stores a JSON document
# and reads one field of it, then deletes the keys.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up valkey

vk=redis://user:password@localhost:6379
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" ping
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" mset 'model:1' '{"a":1}' 'model:2' '{"a":2}'
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" mget 'model:1' 'model:2'

# Store a JSON document with the JSON module and read one field by its path.
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" JSON.SET 'doc:1' '$' '{"name":"odctl","stars":5}'
docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" JSON.GET 'doc:1' '$.stars'

docker exec valkey valkey-cli --no-auth-warning -u "$vk" del 'model:1' 'model:2' 'doc:1'

It prints PONG, OK, the two values, OK, [5] for the stars field and 3 for the three deleted keys.
